questions.q: The law of demand states that, holding other factors constant, an increase in the price of a good will:
options: Increase the quantity demanded
Have no effect on quantity demanded
Increase both demand and supply
Decrease the quantity demanded
questions.explanation: The law of demand holds that price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions, all else equal.

questions.q: The law of supply states that, all else equal, a higher price for a good leads producers to:
options: Supply a smaller quantity
Supply the same quantity
Supply a larger quantity
Exit the market entirely
questions.explanation: Higher prices raise the incentive to produce, so quantity supplied rises with price.

questions.q: Market equilibrium occurs at the price where:
options: Quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
Demand is greater than supply
Supply is greater than demand
Government sets the price by law
questions.explanation: Equilibrium is the price at which the quantity buyers want to buy equals the quantity sellers want to sell.

questions.q: If the market price is set below the equilibrium price, the most likely result is:
options: A surplus of the good
No change in the market
A permanent price increase
A shortage of the good
questions.explanation: Below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, producing a shortage.

questions.q: A price set above equilibrium, such as a binding price floor, typically causes:
options: A shortage
A surplus
Perfect market clearing
Lower production costs
questions.explanation: Above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, creating a surplus (e.g., unsold agricultural produce).

questions.q: A movement ALONG a demand curve is caused by a change in:
options: Consumer income
Consumer tastes
The price of a substitute
The price of the good itself
questions.explanation: Only a change in the good's own price moves you along the curve; other factors shift the whole curve.

questions.q: Which of the following would shift the demand curve for a normal good to the right?
options: A fall in consumer income
A rise in consumer income
An increase in the good's own price
A fall in the number of buyers
questions.explanation: For a normal good, higher income raises demand at every price, shifting the curve rightward.

questions.q: For an inferior good, an increase in consumer income will cause demand to:
options: Increase
Stay exactly the same
Become perfectly elastic
Decrease
questions.explanation: By definition, demand for an inferior good falls as income rises (e.g., cheaper staple grains as households grow richer).

questions.q: Two goods are substitutes if a rise in the price of one causes:
options: A fall in demand for the other
A rise in demand for the other
No change in demand for the other
Both goods to disappear
questions.explanation: When one good becomes costlier, buyers switch to the substitute, raising its demand (e.g., tea and coffee).

questions.q: Two goods are complements if a rise in the price of one causes:
options: A rise in demand for the other
No change for the other
Supply of the other to rise
A fall in demand for the other
questions.explanation: Complements are consumed together, so a price rise in one reduces demand for the other (e.g., cars and petrol).

questions.q: Price elasticity of demand measures:
options: How responsive quantity demanded is to a change in price
The slope of the supply curve
The total revenue of a firm
The cost of producing one more unit
questions.explanation: Elasticity of demand is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.

questions.q: Demand is said to be elastic when the price elasticity of demand is:
options: Equal to zero
Between zero and one
Greater than one (in absolute value)
Exactly equal to one
questions.explanation: Elastic demand means quantity responds more than proportionally to price, giving an elasticity greater than one.

questions.q: If a 10% increase in price causes a 5% fall in quantity demanded, demand is:
options: Elastic
Unit elastic
Perfectly elastic
Inelastic
questions.explanation: The elasticity is 0.5 (less than one), so demand is inelastic: quantity responds less than proportionally.

questions.q: For a good with inelastic demand, a rise in price will cause total revenue to:
options: Fall
Rise
Stay unchanged
Fall to zero
questions.explanation: When demand is inelastic, quantity falls less than price rises, so total revenue increases.

questions.q: Which good is most likely to have highly inelastic demand?
options: A luxury foreign holiday
One particular brand of soft drink
A restaurant meal
A life-saving medicine with no substitute
questions.explanation: Necessities with no substitutes, like essential medicine, have very inelastic demand because buyers cannot easily reduce consumption.

questions.q: Demand tends to be MORE elastic when:
options: The good has many close substitutes
The good is an absolute necessity
The good takes up a tiny share of income
The time horizon is very short
questions.explanation: Availability of close substitutes makes buyers more responsive to price changes, raising elasticity.

questions.q: A perfectly inelastic demand curve is drawn as:
options: A horizontal line
A downward-sloping line
An upward-sloping line
A vertical line
questions.explanation: Perfectly inelastic demand means quantity does not change with price, shown as a vertical line.

questions.q: Income elasticity of demand for a luxury good is:
options: Negative
Zero
Positive and greater than one
Exactly equal to zero
questions.explanation: Luxuries have income elasticity greater than one: demand rises more than proportionally as income grows.

questions.q: Cross-price elasticity of demand between two substitute goods is:
options: Negative
Positive
Always zero
Always exactly one
questions.explanation: For substitutes, a rise in one good's price raises demand for the other, giving a positive cross-price elasticity.

questions.q: Consumer surplus is best defined as:
options: The difference between what consumers pay and what they were willing to pay
The total revenue earned by producers
The cost of producing a good
The tax collected by government
questions.explanation: Consumer surplus is the gap between the maximum a buyer would pay and the price actually paid.

questions.q: Producer surplus is the difference between:
options: Total revenue and total demand
The willingness to pay and the price paid
Fixed cost and variable cost
The price received and the minimum price a producer would accept
questions.explanation: Producer surplus is the amount a seller receives above the lowest price they were willing to accept.

questions.q: On a standard supply-and-demand diagram, consumer surplus is the area:
options: Below the price and above the supply curve
Above the price and below the demand curve
Below both curves
To the right of equilibrium
questions.explanation: Consumer surplus is the triangular area above the market price and below the demand curve.

questions.q: Total economic surplus in a market is the sum of:
options: Consumer surplus and producer surplus
Fixed cost and variable cost
Revenue and profit
Taxes and subsidies
questions.explanation: Total surplus, a measure of market efficiency, equals consumer surplus plus producer surplus.

questions.q: Deadweight loss refers to:
options: The profit earned by a monopoly
The tax revenue collected by the state
The subsidy paid to producers
The loss of total surplus from a market not producing the efficient quantity
questions.explanation: Deadweight loss is the reduction in total surplus caused by producing less (or more) than the efficient quantity.

questions.q: Opportunity cost is best defined as:
options: The money price paid for a good
The value of the next-best alternative foregone
The total cost of all inputs
The interest charged on a loan
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is what you give up, the best alternative, when you choose one option over another.

questions.q: A development NGO can fund either a school or a clinic with a fixed budget, but not both. The opportunity cost of building the school is:
options: The money spent on the school
The salaries of school teachers
Zero, since the budget was fixed
The clinic that was not built
questions.explanation: The opportunity cost is the best foregone alternative: here, the clinic that could have been built instead.

questions.q: The production possibilities frontier (PPF) illustrates:
options: The maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its resources
The demand for a single good
A firm's total revenue
The distribution of income
questions.explanation: The PPF shows the maximum output combinations achievable given fixed resources and technology, illustrating scarcity and trade-offs.

questions.q: A point INSIDE the production possibilities frontier represents:
options: An efficient use of resources
An unattainable combination
Inefficient or underused resources
The optimal outcome
questions.explanation: Points inside the PPF are attainable but inefficient, meaning some resources are idle or misallocated.

questions.q: The bowed-out (concave) shape of a typical PPF reflects:
options: Constant opportunity costs
Increasing opportunity costs
Zero opportunity cost
Decreasing total output
questions.explanation: The concave shape arises because resources are not equally suited to all uses, so opportunity cost rises as more of one good is produced.

questions.q: Marginal cost is defined as:
options: The total cost of production
The cost that does not vary with output
Revenue minus cost
The additional cost of producing one more unit
questions.explanation: Marginal cost is the change in total cost from producing one additional unit of output.

questions.q: Marginal analysis suggests a rational decision-maker should undertake an activity as long as:
options: Total benefit is positive
Marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost
Average cost is falling
Fixed costs are covered
questions.explanation: Optimal decisions are made at the margin: continue while the benefit of one more unit exceeds its cost.

questions.q: A fixed cost is one that:
options: Changes directly with the level of output
Is always larger than variable cost
Only occurs at zero production
Does not change with the level of output in the short run
questions.explanation: Fixed costs, such as rent, remain constant regardless of how much is produced in the short run.

questions.q: Which of the following is a variable cost for a garment factory?
options: Annual rent on the building
Cost of fabric used per shirt
The manager's fixed salary
Insurance premium for the year
questions.explanation: Variable costs change with output; fabric use rises directly with the number of shirts produced.

questions.q: Total cost is equal to:
options: Fixed cost minus variable cost
Fixed cost plus variable cost
Marginal cost times price
Average cost minus profit
questions.explanation: Total cost is the sum of total fixed cost and total variable cost at a given output level.

questions.q: Average total cost is calculated as:
options: Total cost divided by quantity of output
Total cost minus fixed cost
Marginal cost times quantity
Total revenue divided by quantity
questions.explanation: Average total cost is total cost per unit: total cost divided by the number of units produced.

questions.q: A cost that has already been incurred and cannot be recovered is called a:
options: Marginal cost
Sunk cost
Variable cost
Opportunity cost
questions.explanation: Sunk costs are unrecoverable past expenditures and should be ignored in forward-looking decisions.

questions.q: The marginal cost curve typically intersects the average total cost curve at:
options: The maximum point of average total cost
The minimum point of average total cost
The origin
The point where price equals zero
questions.explanation: When marginal cost is below average cost it pulls the average down; the two meet at the minimum of average total cost.

questions.q: The law of diminishing marginal returns states that, as more of a variable input is added to fixed inputs:
options: Total output eventually falls to zero
The additional output from each extra unit of input eventually declines
Marginal cost falls continuously
Fixed costs increase
questions.explanation: Beyond some point, adding more of a variable input yields progressively smaller increases in output.

questions.q: In a perfectly competitive market, an individual firm is a:
options: Price maker
Monopolist
Sole supplier
Price taker
questions.explanation: With many small firms selling identical products, each firm must accept the market price and is a price taker.

questions.q: Which is a defining feature of perfect competition?
options: A single dominant seller
Significant barriers to entry
Many firms selling a homogeneous product
Heavily differentiated products
questions.explanation: Perfect competition features many buyers and sellers, identical products, and free entry and exit.

questions.q: A profit-maximizing firm in any market structure produces the quantity where:
options: Marginal revenue equals marginal cost
Price equals fixed cost
Total revenue is highest regardless of cost
Average cost equals zero
questions.explanation: Profit is maximized where marginal revenue equals marginal cost; beyond this, extra units cost more than they earn.

questions.q: A monopoly is a market structure characterized by:
options: Many firms with identical products
A single seller with significant market power and high barriers to entry
Two large firms
Free entry and exit
questions.explanation: A monopoly has one dominant seller of a product with no close substitutes, protected by barriers to entry.

questions.q: Compared with a competitive market, a monopoly typically produces:
options: A higher quantity at a lower price
The same quantity and price
An infinite quantity
A lower quantity at a higher price
questions.explanation: A monopolist restricts output and charges a higher price than a competitive market, creating deadweight loss.

questions.q: For a monopolist, marginal revenue is:
options: Equal to price
Greater than price
Less than price
Always equal to marginal cost
questions.explanation: Because a monopolist must lower price on all units to sell more, marginal revenue lies below the price.

questions.q: An oligopoly is a market structure in which:
options: A single firm dominates entirely
Thousands of tiny firms compete
There are no barriers to entry
A few large firms dominate the market
questions.explanation: Oligopoly is characterized by a small number of large, interdependent firms (e.g., telecom operators).

questions.q: A key feature that distinguishes oligopoly from other structures is:
options: Perfectly identical products always
Strategic interdependence among firms
The complete absence of market power
An infinite number of sellers
questions.explanation: In oligopoly, each firm's decisions depend on the anticipated reactions of its few rivals: strategic interdependence.

questions.q: When a few firms collude to fix prices or restrict output, they form a:
options: Cartel
Cooperative
Perfectly competitive market
Monopsony
questions.explanation: A cartel is an agreement among firms to coordinate on price or output, behaving collectively like a monopoly.

questions.q: Monopolistic competition differs from perfect competition mainly because firms:
options: Sell identical products
Sell differentiated products and have some price-setting power
Are the only seller in the market
Face no competition at all
questions.explanation: Under monopolistic competition many firms compete, but product differentiation gives each some limited market power.

questions.q: The price mechanism in a market economy primarily serves to:
options: Guarantee equal incomes for all
Allocate scarce resources by signalling and rationing through prices
Eliminate all scarcity
Fix production by government decree
questions.explanation: Prices signal relative scarcity and value, guiding producers and consumers to allocate resources efficiently.

questions.q: A binding minimum wage set above the market-clearing wage is most likely to cause:
options: A shortage of workers
A surplus of labour (unemployment) in that market
Perfect labour market clearing
A fall in the wage rate
questions.explanation: A wage floor above equilibrium raises quantity of labour supplied above quantity demanded, producing unemployment in that market.

questions.q: GDP measures the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given period. What is the key distinction between GDP and GNP (Gross National Product)?
options: GDP counts production within borders regardless of ownership, while GNP counts production by nationals regardless of location
GDP includes only manufactured goods, while GNP includes services too
GDP is measured annually, while GNP is measured quarterly
GDP excludes government spending, while GNP includes it
questions.explanation: GDP is location-based (production inside borders), while GNP is ownership-based (production by a country's nationals, wherever it occurs).

questions.q: GNI (Gross National Income) is increasingly used instead of GNP in international statistics. GNI equals GDP plus which of the following?
options: Net taxes on production
Total remittances sent abroad
Depreciation of fixed capital
Net primary income (compensation and property income) received from abroad
questions.explanation: GNI equals GDP plus net primary income (wages and investment income) received from the rest of the world, making it conceptually close to GNP.

questions.q: For many South Asian economies with large numbers of migrant workers abroad, GNI often exceeds GDP. What is the main reason for this gap?
options: Large trade surpluses in goods
High rates of domestic capital depreciation
Net inflows of workers' remittances and income earned abroad
Government subsidies to exporters
questions.explanation: Substantial remittances and income earned by nationals working overseas add to GNI beyond what is produced domestically (GDP).

questions.q: Nominal GDP is measured at current prices, while real GDP is measured at constant prices. Why do economists prefer real GDP to track growth over time?
options: It includes the informal economy that nominal GDP omits
It is always larger than nominal GDP
It counts intermediate goods that nominal GDP ignores
It removes the effect of price changes, isolating changes in actual output
questions.explanation: Real GDP holds prices constant so that measured changes reflect real output growth rather than inflation.

questions.q: The GDP deflator is a measure of the price level calculated as which ratio?
options: Real GDP divided by nominal GDP, times 100
GDP divided by population
Nominal GDP divided by real GDP, times 100
The consumer price index divided by the wholesale price index
questions.explanation: The GDP deflator equals (nominal GDP / real GDP) × 100 and reflects prices of all domestically produced goods and services.

questions.q: In the expenditure approach to national income accounting, GDP is the sum of consumption, investment, government spending, and net exports. Net exports is defined as which of the following?
options: Exports minus imports
Exports plus imports
Imports minus exports
Total value of exports only
questions.explanation: Net exports equals exports minus imports; imports are subtracted because they are produced abroad, not domestically.

questions.q: GDP is widely criticized as a welfare measure. Which of the following does standard GDP fail to capture?
options: The market value of exported manufactured goods
Government expenditure on public services
Private investment in new factories
Unpaid household and care work, environmental degradation, and income distribution
questions.explanation: GDP omits non-market activity like unpaid care work, ignores environmental costs, and says nothing about how income is distributed.

questions.q: The Human Development Index (HDI) was designed as an alternative to purely income-based measures. Which three dimensions does the HDI combine?
options: Health (life expectancy), education, and standard of living (income)
Income, inequality, and unemployment
Health, environment, and governance
Inflation, growth, and trade openness
questions.explanation: The HDI aggregates life expectancy, education (schooling), and gross national income per capita into a single index.

questions.q: Economic growth and economic development are related but distinct. Which statement best captures the difference?
options: Growth refers to rising output, while development includes broader improvements in living standards, capabilities, and equity
Growth and development are identical concepts measured differently
Development refers only to industrialization, while growth refers to agriculture
Growth is qualitative, while development is purely quantitative
questions.explanation: Growth is a quantitative rise in output; development is a broader, qualitative process improving well-being, capabilities, and distribution.

questions.q: Amartya Sen's capability approach reframed development. According to Sen, development is best understood as which of the following?
options: Maximization of per capita GDP
The expansion of people's real freedoms and capabilities to lead lives they value
The accumulation of physical capital
The growth of exports and foreign reserves
questions.explanation: Sen defined development as the expansion of substantive freedoms and capabilities, not merely income or output growth.

questions.q: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures the average change over time in prices paid by consumers for a basket of goods and services. What is a well-known limitation of CPI as an inflation measure?
options: It updates the basket weights every month
It excludes food and housing entirely
It can overstate inflation by not fully accounting for substitution and quality improvements
It measures only wholesale transactions
questions.explanation: A fixed basket ignores consumers substituting away from costlier goods and quality gains, tending to overstate the true cost-of-living rise.

questions.q: India transitioned to using CPI as its primary inflation target measure, but historically relied heavily on another index for headline inflation. Which index was that?
options: The GDP deflator
The Producer Price Index (PPI)
The Wholesale Price Index (WPI)
The Big Mac Index
questions.explanation: India long headlined the Wholesale Price Index before adopting CPI as the inflation-targeting benchmark under its monetary policy framework.

questions.q: Core inflation is a concept central banks watch closely. How does core inflation differ from headline inflation?
options: Core inflation includes taxes, while headline excludes them
Core inflation measures only imported goods
Core inflation excludes volatile items like food and fuel prices
Core inflation is always higher than headline inflation
questions.explanation: Core inflation strips out volatile food and energy prices to reveal the underlying, more persistent inflation trend.

questions.q: Hyperinflation refers to extremely rapid price increases. Which of the following is a typical consequence of hyperinflation?
options: Erosion of money's value, collapse of savings, and flight to foreign currency or barter
Strengthening of the domestic currency
Rising real wages for workers
Increased confidence in long-term contracts
questions.explanation: Hyperinflation destroys the value of money, wiping out savings and pushing people toward foreign currency, hard assets, or barter.

questions.q: Deflation is a sustained fall in the general price level. Why do economists often consider deflation dangerous?
options: It can raise the real burden of debt and cause consumers to delay spending, deepening recessions
It always boosts consumer spending immediately
It automatically increases exports
It has no effect on real interest rates
questions.explanation: Falling prices raise the real value of debts and encourage postponed purchases, which can trap an economy in a downward spiral.

questions.q: The distinction between real and nominal interest rates matters for borrowers and savers. According to the Fisher equation, the real interest rate is approximately equal to which of the following?
options: The nominal interest rate plus expected inflation
Expected inflation minus the nominal interest rate
The nominal interest rate minus expected inflation
The nominal interest rate times expected inflation
questions.explanation: The Fisher relation states the real rate approximately equals the nominal interest rate minus expected inflation.

questions.q: The unemployment rate is a key labor market indicator. How is it conventionally calculated?
options: Unemployed persons divided by the total population
Unemployed persons divided by the number of employed
Unemployed persons divided by the working-age population
Unemployed persons divided by the labor force (employed plus unemployed)
questions.explanation: The unemployment rate is the number of unemployed divided by the labor force, expressed as a percentage.

questions.q: A person who has given up looking for work because they believe none is available is classified in labor statistics as which of the following?
options: A discouraged worker, typically counted outside the labor force
Frictionally unemployed
Structurally unemployed and counted in the labor force
Underemployed but fully employed
questions.explanation: Discouraged workers have stopped searching and are excluded from the labor force, so official unemployment understates joblessness.

questions.q: Structural unemployment differs from cyclical unemployment. Which scenario best illustrates structural unemployment?
options: A worker laid off during a recession who is rehired when demand recovers
A textile worker whose skills no longer match jobs after automation reshapes the industry
A graduate spending a few weeks searching for their first job
A seasonal farm worker between harvests
questions.explanation: Structural unemployment arises from a mismatch between workers' skills or location and available jobs, often due to technological or industry change.

questions.q: In many South Asian economies, a large share of employment is in the informal sector. What does this imply for standard unemployment statistics?
options: Unemployment rates fully capture labor market distress
Informal workers are always counted as unemployed
The labor force participation rate is irrelevant
Low official unemployment can mask widespread underemployment and low-quality informal work
questions.explanation: With few social safety nets, people take any informal work to survive, so low measured unemployment hides underemployment and poor job quality.

questions.q: The labor force participation rate is an important complement to the unemployment rate. It is defined as which of the following?
options: The share of the total population that is employed
The share of employed people who work full time
The share of unemployed people receiving benefits
The share of the working-age population that is either employed or actively seeking work
questions.explanation: The participation rate is the labor force (employed plus actively job-seeking) as a share of the working-age population.

questions.q: Female labor force participation in India has been notably low and even declining in some periods. Which factor is commonly cited as a contributor?
options: An acute shortage of working-age women
Universally high female wages discouraging work
Social norms, unpaid care burdens, and lack of suitable/safe job opportunities
Mandatory retirement of women at age 40
questions.explanation: Care responsibilities, social norms, safety concerns, and limited quality jobs all depress measured female participation in India.

questions.q: Fiscal policy refers to government use of which two main instruments to influence the economy?
options: Interest rates and reserve requirements
Government spending and taxation
Exchange rates and tariffs
The money supply and open market operations
questions.explanation: Fiscal policy operates through government spending and taxation decisions, typically set in the budget.

questions.q: During a recession, a government pursuing expansionary fiscal policy would most likely do which of the following?
options: Raise taxes and cut spending to balance the budget
Raise interest rates to attract capital
Reduce the money supply to control inflation
Increase government spending and/or cut taxes to boost aggregate demand
questions.explanation: Expansionary fiscal policy raises demand by increasing spending or cutting taxes, running a larger deficit to stimulate the economy.

questions.q: The fiscal deficit is a closely watched indicator in South Asian budgets. It is best defined as which of the following?
options: The total accumulated debt of the government
The gap between exports and imports
The difference between tax revenue and defense spending
The excess of total government expenditure over total revenue (excluding borrowing) in a year
questions.explanation: The fiscal deficit is the shortfall of revenues against expenditures in a year, financed by borrowing; accumulated deficits form the public debt.

questions.q: Automatic stabilizers help smooth the business cycle without new legislation. Which of the following is an example of an automatic stabilizer?
options: A one-time infrastructure stimulus package passed by parliament
A central bank interest rate cut
Progressive income taxes and unemployment benefits that adjust with the economy
A currency devaluation
questions.explanation: Progressive taxes fall and welfare payments rise automatically in downturns, cushioning demand without new policy action.

questions.q: The fiscal multiplier is central to debates about stimulus. What does a fiscal multiplier greater than one imply?
options: Government spending has no effect on output
A unit increase in government spending raises total output by more than one unit
Taxes rise faster than spending
The budget must always be balanced
questions.explanation: A multiplier above one means each rupee of government spending generates more than a rupee of additional GDP through induced spending.

questions.q: Crowding out is a concern raised against deficit-financed government spending. What does crowding out refer to?
options: Government spending directly increasing private consumption
Government borrowing raising interest rates and reducing private investment
Foreign investors leaving the bond market
Inflation eroding the value of tax revenue
questions.explanation: Crowding out occurs when heavy government borrowing pushes up interest rates, discouraging private investment.

questions.q: Monetary policy is typically conducted by a central bank. Which institution conducts monetary policy in India?
options: The Reserve Bank of India
The Ministry of Finance
The Securities and Exchange Board of India
The NITI Aayog
questions.explanation: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is the central bank responsible for conducting India's monetary policy.

questions.q: Many central banks, including the RBI, use inflation targeting. Under inflation targeting, the central bank primarily commits to which of the following?
options: Maintaining a fixed exchange rate at all costs
Keeping inflation near a publicly announced target rate
Maximizing government revenue
Guaranteeing full employment regardless of prices
questions.explanation: Inflation targeting anchors policy around achieving a publicly stated inflation rate, guiding expectations and interest rate decisions.

questions.q: The policy repo rate is the RBI's key instrument. What is the repo rate?
options: The rate at which the RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks against securities
The rate banks pay depositors
The tax rate on bank profits
The exchange rate of the rupee against the dollar
questions.explanation: The repo rate is the rate at which commercial banks borrow short-term from the central bank against government securities, influencing overall lending rates.

questions.q: When a central bank wants to slow an overheating economy and curb inflation, it typically does which of the following?
options: Lowers the policy interest rate
Prints more currency directly for the government
Reduces reserve requirements for banks
Raises the policy interest rate to make borrowing costlier and cool demand
questions.explanation: Raising the policy rate increases borrowing costs, dampening credit, spending, and demand-driven inflation.

questions.q: Open market operations are a standard monetary policy tool. When a central bank buys government bonds in the open market, what is the immediate effect?
options: It increases the money supply and tends to lower interest rates
It reduces the money supply and raises interest rates
It has no effect on liquidity
It directly lowers the fiscal deficit
questions.explanation: Buying bonds injects money into the banking system, expanding the money supply and putting downward pressure on interest rates.

questions.q: The Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) is a monetary tool used by the RBI. What does raising the CRR do?
options: Increases the funds banks can lend
Lowers the interest rate banks charge
Requires banks to hold more reserves, reducing funds available for lending
Directly increases government spending
questions.explanation: A higher CRR forces banks to park more deposits with the central bank, shrinking loanable funds and tightening credit.

questions.q: Quantitative easing (QE) is an unconventional monetary policy. When is it typically deployed?
options: When inflation is dangerously high
When the government runs a budget surplus
When exchange rates are fixed
When policy interest rates are near zero and further conventional easing is limited
questions.explanation: QE, large-scale asset purchases, is used when short-term rates are already near zero, to inject liquidity and lower long-term rates.

questions.q: The nominal exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another. If the Indian rupee 'depreciates' against the US dollar, what has happened?
options: It takes fewer rupees to buy one dollar
It takes more rupees to buy one dollar
The dollar has weakened against the rupee
Indian exports become more expensive abroad
questions.explanation: Depreciation means the rupee has lost value, so more rupees are needed to purchase one dollar.

questions.q: A currency depreciation affects trade. In general, a weaker domestic currency tends to have which effect?
options: Make exports more expensive and imports cheaper
Have no effect on the trade balance
Make exports cheaper and imports more expensive
Automatically eliminate the current account deficit
questions.explanation: A weaker currency lowers the foreign-currency price of exports and raises the domestic price of imports, tending to boost net exports.

questions.q: Under a fixed (pegged) exchange rate regime, how does a central bank maintain the peg?
options: By letting the currency float freely
By buying and selling foreign reserves to keep the exchange rate at the target level
By raising income taxes
By ignoring the foreign exchange market
questions.explanation: To hold a peg, the central bank intervenes in the forex market, buying or selling reserves to offset market pressures on the currency.

questions.q: Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) is used to compare living standards across countries. What is the core idea behind PPP-adjusted GDP comparisons?
options: They adjust for differences in the cost of living so that GDPs reflect real purchasing power
Currencies should be compared only at market exchange rates
They ignore price differences between countries
They measure only tradable goods
questions.explanation: PPP adjusts for price-level differences, so incomes are compared in terms of what they can actually buy across countries.

questions.q: The current account of the balance of payments records several types of transactions. Which of the following is a component of the current account?
options: Foreign direct investment inflows
The trade balance in goods and services plus net income and transfers
Purchases of foreign government bonds
Changes in official foreign exchange reserves
questions.explanation: The current account covers trade in goods and services, net primary income, and net transfers such as remittances; investment flows sit in the capital/financial account.

questions.q: The business cycle describes fluctuations in economic activity. Which sequence correctly orders the phases of a typical business cycle?
options: Peak, expansion, trough, contraction
Expansion, peak, contraction (recession), trough
Trough, contraction, peak, expansion
Contraction, trough, peak, expansion
questions.explanation: A cycle typically moves from expansion to a peak, then contraction (recession) down to a trough, before recovering.

questions.q: A recession is commonly defined by a rule of thumb involving GDP. What is that common definition?
options: A single quarter of falling employment
Any year in which inflation exceeds 5 percent
A fall in the stock market of more than 10 percent
Two consecutive quarters of declining real GDP
questions.explanation: The popular rule of thumb defines a recession as two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP, though official bodies use broader criteria.

questions.q: Aggregate demand is a core macroeconomic concept. Which of the following would shift the aggregate demand curve to the right?
options: A rise in interest rates
A fall in exports
An increase in consumer confidence and government spending
An increase in income taxes
questions.explanation: Higher consumer confidence and government spending raise total planned expenditure, shifting aggregate demand outward.

questions.q: The Phillips curve describes a relationship between two macroeconomic variables. Which relationship does the traditional short-run Phillips curve depict?
options: A positive relationship between growth and inflation
A positive relationship between unemployment and inflation
An inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation
No relationship between employment and prices
questions.explanation: The short-run Phillips curve posits an inverse trade-off: lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation, and vice versa.

questions.q: Stagflation challenged simple Phillips curve thinking in the 1970s. What defines stagflation?
options: Simultaneous high inflation and high unemployment (stagnant growth)
High growth combined with low inflation
Falling prices with rising output
Full employment with zero inflation
questions.explanation: Stagflation is the coexistence of stagnant growth/high unemployment with high inflation, contradicting a stable inflation-unemployment trade-off.

questions.q: The Solow growth model highlights the role of a particular factor in sustaining long-run per capita growth. According to Solow, sustained long-run growth in output per worker depends mainly on which of the following?
options: Continuous capital accumulation alone
Population growth
Rising government deficits
Technological progress (total factor productivity)
questions.explanation: Because of diminishing returns to capital, the Solow model shows that sustained per capita growth ultimately requires technological progress.

questions.q: The 'middle-income trap' is a concern for developing economies. What does it describe?
options: A country stuck in extreme poverty unable to grow at all
A country that reaches middle-income levels but stalls, unable to advance to high-income status
A country with permanently high inflation
A country that grows too fast and overheats
questions.explanation: The middle-income trap describes economies that stagnate after reaching middle-income levels, losing low-wage competitiveness without gaining high-productivity industries.

questions.q: Gross Capital Formation (investment) is a key driver of growth. In national accounts, which of the following counts as investment?
options: A household buying government bonds
A firm purchasing new machinery and building a new factory
A person buying shares on the stock exchange
The government paying pension benefits
questions.explanation: In macroeconomics, investment means additions to the physical capital stock (new machinery, structures, and inventories) not financial asset purchases.

questions.q: The savings-investment identity is fundamental in a closed economy. In such an economy at equilibrium, national saving equals which of the following?
options: Government spending
Investment
Net exports
Consumption
questions.explanation: In a closed economy, total saving must equal total investment, an accounting identity underlying growth and capital formation.

questions.q: Development economists increasingly emphasize inclusive growth. Which statement best describes inclusive growth?
options: Growth that broadly raises living standards and creates opportunities across income groups, including the poor
Growth measured only by rising GDP per capita
Growth concentrated in the financial sector
Growth that prioritizes exports over all else
questions.explanation: Inclusive growth spreads the benefits of expansion across society, especially to the poor and marginalized, through jobs, access, and reduced inequality.

questions.q: An allocation of resources is said to be Pareto efficient when:
options: Total output in the economy is maximized regardless of distribution
No one can be made better off without making at least one other person worse off
Everyone in society has an equal share of resources
The government has redistributed income to reduce poverty
questions.explanation: Pareto efficiency means no reallocation can improve one person's welfare without harming another's.

questions.q: A Pareto improvement is a change that:
options: Makes at least one person better off and no one worse off
Increases total GDP even if some lose
Equalizes incomes across the population
Reduces the government's fiscal deficit
questions.explanation: A Pareto improvement benefits at least one party while leaving no one worse off.

questions.q: A key limitation of the Pareto criterion for development policy is that it:
options: Cannot be applied to competitive markets
Requires perfect equality to be satisfied
Says nothing about fairness or the distribution of welfare
Only works when there is a single consumer
questions.explanation: An allocation can be Pareto efficient yet highly unequal, so the criterion ignores distributive justice.

questions.q: The First Fundamental Theorem of Welfare Economics states that:
options: Any Pareto efficient allocation can be reached through redistribution
Markets always maximize social equality
Government intervention always improves efficiency
Any competitive market equilibrium is Pareto efficient under certain conditions
questions.explanation: The First Welfare Theorem shows competitive equilibria are Pareto efficient absent market failures.

questions.q: The Second Fundamental Theorem of Welfare Economics implies that:
options: Any Pareto efficient allocation can be achieved as a market equilibrium with appropriate lump-sum transfers
Redistribution is always impossible without efficiency losses
Markets can never be efficient
Public goods are always provided optimally
questions.explanation: The Second Welfare Theorem separates efficiency from distribution via lump-sum redistribution of endowments.

questions.q: A negative externality occurs when:
options: A firm earns higher profits than expected
A third party bears costs from a transaction they were not part of
Consumers receive a subsidy from the government
A market reaches competitive equilibrium
questions.explanation: Negative externalities impose uncompensated costs on third parties, as with factory pollution.

questions.q: When a factory emits pollution that harms downstream farmers, the market outcome typically features:
options: Underproduction relative to the socially optimal level
Production exactly at the social optimum
Overproduction relative to the socially optimal level
No production at all
questions.explanation: Because polluters ignore external costs, the good is overproduced beyond the social optimum.

questions.q: A positive externality, such as a household vaccinating its children, tends to be:
options: Overprovided by the market relative to the social optimum
Underprovided by the market relative to the social optimum
Provided exactly at the social optimum
Fully priced into the market
questions.explanation: Since private actors ignore benefits to others, goods with positive externalities are underprovided.

questions.q: For a good with a negative externality, the marginal social cost is:
options: Less than the marginal private cost
Equal to the marginal private cost
Always zero
Greater than the marginal private cost
questions.explanation: Social cost equals private cost plus the external cost, so it exceeds private cost.

questions.q: A Pigouvian tax is designed to:
options: Maximize government revenue from all industries
Make polluters internalize the external cost by setting the tax equal to marginal external damage
Subsidize firms that create pollution
Ban production of harmful goods outright
questions.explanation: A Pigouvian tax equal to marginal external damage aligns private and social costs.

questions.q: A Pigouvian subsidy is an appropriate response to:
options: A negative externality that is overprovided
A natural monopoly
A positive externality that is underprovided by the market
Perfectly competitive equilibrium
questions.explanation: Subsidizing activities with positive externalities encourages provision toward the social optimum.

questions.q: The two defining characteristics of a pure public good are that it is:
options: Rival and excludable in consumption
Provided only by private firms
Always priced above marginal cost
Non-rival and non-excludable in consumption
questions.explanation: Pure public goods are non-rival (one person's use does not reduce another's) and non-excludable.

questions.q: Which of the following is the best example of a pure public good?
options: National defense
A loaf of bread
A toll highway
A cinema seat
questions.explanation: National defense is non-rival and non-excludable, the hallmarks of a pure public good.

questions.q: The free-rider problem arises because:
options: Firms charge too high a price for public goods
People can benefit from a non-excludable good without paying for it
Governments always overprovide public goods
Consumers cannot enjoy the good simultaneously
questions.explanation: Non-excludability lets individuals consume the good without contributing, undermining voluntary provision.

questions.q: The free-rider problem leads private markets to:
options: Overprovide public goods
Provide public goods at the optimal level
Underprovide public goods relative to the socially optimal level
Charge marginal cost for public goods
questions.explanation: Because people withhold payment, voluntary contributions fall short of efficient provision.

questions.q: A good that is rival but non-excludable is classified as a:
options: Pure public good
Common-pool resource
Pure private good
Club good
questions.explanation: Common-pool resources are rival in consumption yet difficult to exclude users from, like fisheries.

questions.q: A good that is non-rival but excludable is best described as a:
options: Common-pool resource
Pure public good
Pure private good
Club good
questions.explanation: Club goods, such as subscription streaming, are non-rival up to congestion but exclude non-payers.

questions.q: The 'tragedy of the commons' refers to:
options: The tendency of governments to nationalize all industries
Overexploitation of a shared resource because individual users ignore the cost imposed on others
Underuse of public parks due to high fees
The efficient private management of forests
questions.explanation: Open access leads each user to overexploit, degrading the shared resource for all.

questions.q: Elinor Ostrom's research on common-pool resources showed that:
options: Communities can sustainably self-govern shared resources through local institutions and rules
Only state ownership can prevent resource depletion
Only full privatization prevents the tragedy of the commons
Common-pool resources are always overexploited
questions.explanation: Ostrom documented that local user-managed institutions can avert the commons tragedy without state or market.

questions.q: Asymmetric information exists in a transaction when:
options: Both parties are equally uninformed
One party has more or better information than the other
The government withholds data from firms
Prices are set by a central planner
questions.explanation: Asymmetric information means one side of the transaction knows more than the other.

questions.q: Adverse selection is a problem that occurs:
options: After a transaction, when behavior changes
Only in perfectly competitive markets
Before a transaction, when hidden characteristics distort who participates in the market
When information is symmetric
questions.explanation: Adverse selection arises from hidden information before contracting, skewing the pool of participants.

questions.q: Akerlof's 'market for lemons' illustrates how asymmetric information can cause:
options: High-quality goods to be driven out of the market
Prices to always reflect true quality
Buyers to have more information than sellers
Markets to reach perfect efficiency
questions.explanation: When buyers cannot verify quality, they offer low prices, driving out good used cars ('lemons' remain).

questions.q: Moral hazard refers to a situation where:
options: A buyer knows less than a seller before a sale
A party changes its behavior after a contract because it does not bear the full consequences
Two firms collude to raise prices
The government provides a public good
questions.explanation: Moral hazard is a post-contract problem: insured or protected parties take on more risk.

questions.q: A fully insured driver who drives less carefully than an uninsured driver is an example of:
options: Adverse selection
A positive externality
Moral hazard
The free-rider problem
questions.explanation: Reduced care after obtaining insurance is classic moral hazard from changed behavior.

questions.q: In health insurance, the tendency for sicker individuals to be more likely to buy coverage reflects:
options: Adverse selection
Moral hazard
A Pigouvian externality
A public good problem
questions.explanation: Higher-risk people self-selecting into insurance before contracting is adverse selection.

questions.q: 'Signaling', as in job-market education, is a market response to:
options: A negative production externality
The free-rider problem
A natural monopoly
Asymmetric information, where the informed party reveals hidden quality
questions.explanation: Signaling lets the informed party (e.g., a worker) credibly convey unobservable quality to the uninformed.

questions.q: 'Screening' differs from signaling in that it is undertaken by:
options: The uninformed party to sort the informed party by type
The government to raise revenue
The informed party to reveal its type
A monopolist to raise prices
questions.explanation: In screening the uninformed side designs mechanisms (e.g., insurance menus) to separate types.

questions.q: Merit goods are goods that policymakers believe:
options: Should never be provided by the state
Are under-consumed relative to what is socially desirable, often due to imperfect information
Are always over-consumed by rational consumers
Have no external benefits
questions.explanation: Merit goods like education and vaccination are deemed under-consumed and are often subsidized.

questions.q: A demerit good is one that is considered to be:
options: Under-consumed relative to the social optimum
A pure public good
Over-consumed relative to the socially desirable level, such as tobacco
Free from any externalities
questions.explanation: Demerit goods such as tobacco are over-consumed and often taxed or regulated.

questions.q: The Coase theorem states that if property rights are well-defined and transaction costs are:
options: Very high, government must always intervene
Zero, only the government can resolve externalities
Positive, bargaining always fails
Zero, private parties can bargain to an efficient outcome regardless of the initial allocation of rights
questions.explanation: With clear rights and no transaction costs, private bargaining internalizes externalities efficiently.

questions.q: According to the Coase theorem, the initial assignment of property rights affects:
options: The distribution of income but not the efficiency of the final outcome
Neither efficiency nor distribution
Only efficiency, never distribution
Nothing at all
questions.explanation: Coase showed the efficient outcome is reached either way; only who pays whom (distribution) changes.

questions.q: The Coase theorem's practical relevance is often limited in development contexts because:
options: Property rights are always perfectly clear
There are never any externalities
Transaction costs are high and property rights are poorly defined
Bargaining is costless in villages
questions.explanation: High transaction costs and weak or contested property rights undermine Coasean bargaining in practice.

questions.q: A cap-and-trade system controls pollution by:
options: Setting a total emissions limit and allowing firms to trade permits
Banning all industrial production
Subsidizing polluters directly
Fixing the price of every good
questions.explanation: Cap-and-trade caps total emissions and lets tradable permits allocate abatement to lowest-cost firms.

questions.q: A natural monopoly arises when:
options: Many small firms compete perfectly
A single firm can supply the entire market at lower cost than multiple firms due to economies of scale
The government owns all firms
Information is perfectly symmetric
questions.explanation: Natural monopolies feature declining average costs so one firm serves the market most cheaply.

questions.q: Government failure refers to a situation where:
options: Markets always outperform government
The government perfectly corrects all market failures
State intervention produces outcomes worse than or as inefficient as the market failure it addresses
There is no role for public policy
questions.explanation: Government failure occurs when intervention itself creates inefficiency, capture, or unintended harm.

questions.q: 'Regulatory capture' occurs when:
options: A regulatory agency serves the interests of the industry it is meant to oversee
Consumers gain full control of prices
The government eliminates all regulations
Markets become perfectly competitive
questions.explanation: Regulatory capture is when regulated firms co-opt the regulator, undermining the public interest.

questions.q: 'Rent-seeking' behavior refers to:
options: Landlords collecting rent from tenants
Efforts to gain income through favorable policy or privilege rather than productive activity
Firms lowering prices to compete
Consumers saving money
questions.explanation: Rent-seeking uses resources to capture existing wealth via lobbying rather than create new value.

questions.q: The 'deadweight loss' from a market failure represents:
options: The profit earned by monopolists
Total government tax revenue
The consumer surplus at equilibrium
The loss of total surplus from producing at a quantity other than the social optimum
questions.explanation: Deadweight loss measures the surplus destroyed when output deviates from the efficient level.

questions.q: In the presence of a negative externality, a corrective tax improves welfare by:
options: Reducing output toward the social optimum and cutting the external harm
Increasing output beyond the private equilibrium
Eliminating all producer surplus
Raising the deadweight loss
questions.explanation: A corrective tax curtails overproduction, shrinking external damage and deadweight loss.

questions.q: Lindahl pricing is a theoretical scheme to finance public goods by:
options: Charging everyone the same flat fee
Charging each person according to their marginal benefit from the good
Using only voluntary donations
Selling the good at market price
questions.explanation: Lindahl prices set individual charges equal to marginal benefit, yielding efficient public-good provision.

questions.q: The condition for the efficient provision of a public good (Samuelson condition) is that:
options: The sum of individuals' marginal benefits equals the marginal cost of provision
Each person's marginal benefit equals marginal cost
Marginal benefit is zero
Price equals average cost
questions.explanation: For non-rival goods, marginal benefits are summed vertically and set equal to marginal cost.

questions.q: Command-and-control regulation of pollution refers to:
options: Letting firms trade emission permits freely
Imposing a per-unit tax on emissions
Government mandating specific technologies or emission limits directly
Relying solely on private bargaining
questions.explanation: Command-and-control sets prescriptive standards or technology requirements rather than market incentives.

questions.q: A key advantage of market-based instruments (taxes, permits) over command-and-control is that they:
options: Guarantee zero pollution
Achieve pollution reduction at lower total cost by equalizing marginal abatement costs
Require no information about firms
Eliminate the need for property rights
questions.explanation: Market instruments let low-cost abaters cut more, minimizing the total cost of a given reduction.

questions.q: In a common-pool fishery with open access, individual fishers tend to:
options: Catch less than the social optimum
Catch exactly the sustainable yield
Stop fishing entirely
Catch more than the socially optimal amount because they ignore the effect on others' catches
questions.explanation: Each fisher ignores the congestion externality imposed on others, causing over-harvesting.

questions.q: 'Missing markets' are a source of market failure because:
options: Too many firms enter every market
Some goods (like certain insurance or environmental services) are not traded at all, leaving needs unmet
Prices are always set correctly
Governments trade every good
questions.explanation: When markets for certain goods fail to exist, potential welfare-improving trades never occur.

questions.q: A price ceiling set below the market equilibrium price typically causes:
options: A surplus of the good
No effect on the market
A shortage, as quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
A rise in the equilibrium price
questions.explanation: Binding price ceilings hold price below equilibrium, so demand outstrips supply and shortages emerge.

questions.q: Compared with the Pareto criterion, the Kaldor-Hicks criterion judges a change desirable if:
options: The gainers could in principle compensate the losers and still be better off
No one is made worse off at all
Incomes become perfectly equal
The government gains revenue
questions.explanation: Kaldor-Hicks (potential compensation) allows some to lose if gainers' gains could hypothetically offset losses.

questions.q: A social welfare function is used in welfare economics to:
options: Measure only total GDP
Rank different allocations by aggregating individual welfare according to a value judgment
Guarantee Pareto efficiency automatically
Eliminate the need for prices
questions.explanation: A social welfare function embeds distributional values to rank allocations beyond mere efficiency.

questions.q: Which policy instrument most directly addresses the free-rider problem in providing a pure public good?
options: A voluntary donation drive
A Pigouvian tax on producers
Government provision financed through compulsory taxation
Assigning tradable pollution permits
questions.explanation: Compulsory taxation overcomes free-riding by forcing everyone to contribute to the public good.

questions.q: A congestion charge on vehicles entering a crowded city center is best understood as:
options: A subsidy for a positive externality
A Pigouvian charge that internalizes the negative externality of congestion
A method to provide a pure public good
A tool that creates adverse selection
questions.explanation: Drivers impose delay costs on others; a congestion charge forces them to internalize that externality.

questions.q: The headcount ratio (H) in poverty measurement is defined as:
options: The total number of people in a country regardless of income
The proportion of the population living below the poverty line
The average income shortfall of the poor below the poverty line
The ratio of the richest decile's income to the poorest decile's income
questions.explanation: The headcount ratio measures the share of the population whose income or consumption falls below the poverty line.

questions.q: A key limitation of the headcount ratio as a poverty measure is that it:
options: Overstates poverty in high-income countries
Requires household consumption data which is unavailable
Cannot be calculated for rural areas
Is insensitive to how far below the poverty line the poor actually are
questions.explanation: The headcount ratio ignores the depth of poverty: a poor person getting poorer does not change H at all.

questions.q: The poverty gap index measures:
options: The number of people just above the poverty line
The gap between the richest and poorest households
The difference between rural and urban poverty rates
The average shortfall of the poor from the poverty line, expressed relative to the line
questions.explanation: The poverty gap index captures the depth of poverty by averaging the normalized income shortfalls of the poor across the whole population.

questions.q: An absolute poverty line is best described as one that is:
options: Set as a fixed percentage of median income
Recalculated each year as half the mean income
Determined by public opinion surveys on adequacy
Anchored to a fixed basket of goods needed for basic subsistence
questions.explanation: Absolute poverty lines are anchored to the cost of a fixed minimum bundle of essential goods, independent of the overall income distribution.

questions.q: A relative poverty line is typically defined as:
options: A threshold such as 50% or 60% of the median income
A fixed dollar-a-day international standard
The cost of 2100 calories per person per day
The minimum wage set by the government
questions.explanation: Relative poverty lines are set relative to the income distribution, commonly at 50–60% of median income, capturing exclusion rather than subsistence.

questions.q: In India, the Tendulkar Committee (2009) recommended a poverty line based primarily on:
options: Half the median national consumption
A basket covering food, education, and health expenditure, moving away from calorie-only norms
A fixed 2400 rural calorie norm alone
The international $1.90 PPP line
questions.explanation: The Tendulkar line shifted from a pure calorie norm to a broader consumption basket including spending on health and education.

questions.q: The Rangarajan Committee (2014) poverty line, compared with the Tendulkar line, generally produced:
options: An identical estimate
No estimate for urban areas
A higher poverty estimate due to a higher threshold
A lower poverty estimate
questions.explanation: The Rangarajan Committee set higher monthly per-capita expenditure thresholds, raising the estimated number of poor above Tendulkar figures.

questions.q: The Gini coefficient ranges between:
options: 1 and 10, where 1 is perfect equality
0 and 1, where 0 is perfect equality
-1 and +1, where 0 is neutral
0 and 100 always, never expressed as a fraction
questions.explanation: The Gini coefficient runs from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality), though it is sometimes multiplied by 100 as an index.

questions.q: The Lorenz curve plots:
options: Calorie intake against household size
Cumulative share of income against cumulative share of population
Income against consumption for each individual
Poverty rate against year
questions.explanation: The Lorenz curve maps the cumulative percentage of total income received against the cumulative percentage of the population, from poorest to richest.

questions.q: On a Lorenz curve diagram, perfect equality is represented by:
options: The 45-degree diagonal line
A horizontal line at the bottom
A vertical line at the far right
A curve bowed toward the bottom-right corner
questions.explanation: The 45-degree line of equality shows each population share receiving an equal income share; actual Lorenz curves bow below it.

questions.q: The Gini coefficient is geometrically equal to:
options: The area under the Lorenz curve
The distance from the origin to the Lorenz curve
The slope of the Lorenz curve at its midpoint
The ratio of the area between the equality line and the Lorenz curve to the total area under the equality line
questions.explanation: The Gini equals area A (between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve) divided by area A+B (the whole triangle under the equality line).

questions.q: The global Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) developed by OPHI and UNDP is composed of three dimensions:
options: Food, water, and sanitation only
Health, education, and standard of living
Employment, housing, and transport
Income, wealth, and savings
questions.explanation: The global MPI aggregates ten indicators grouped into three equally weighted dimensions: health, education, and living standards.

questions.q: The MPI value is calculated as the product of:
options: Headcount ratio (H) and intensity of deprivation (A)
Calorie norm and food price index
Gini and poverty gap
Mean income and population size
questions.explanation: MPI = H × A, where H is the share of people who are multidimensionally poor and A is the average share of weighted deprivations they experience.

questions.q: In the global MPI methodology, a person is identified as multidimensionally poor if their weighted deprivation score is at least:
options: One-third (33.3%)
questions.explanation: The MPI uses a deprivation cutoff of one-third: a person deprived in a third or more of the weighted indicators is counted as poor.

questions.q: India's national MPI, published by NITI Aayog, draws its underlying indicator data primarily from:
options: The Annual Survey of Industries
The Economic Census
The Census of India population count
The National Family Health Survey (NFHS)
questions.explanation: India's National MPI uses NFHS data to measure deprivations in health, education, and standard of living.

questions.q: Sen's capability approach argues that well-being should be assessed in terms of:
options: The market value of assets owned
Total household income only
A person's capabilities: the real freedoms to achieve valued functionings
Calorie intake per capita exclusively
questions.explanation: Amartya Sen frames development as the expansion of capabilities: the substantive freedoms people have to lead lives they value.

questions.q: In Sen's framework, 'functionings' refer to:
options: The mathematical functions used to compute poverty lines
The functions of government welfare departments
The various things a person actually manages to do or be, such as being nourished or literate
The productive functions of firms in an economy
questions.explanation: Functionings are the achieved states and activities (beings and doings) a person realizes, while capabilities are the sets of functionings they could achieve.

questions.q: A central reason Sen preferred capabilities over income as a metric is that:
options: People differ in their ability to convert income into valuable functionings
Capabilities are easier to count than rupees
Income cannot be measured in developing countries
Income data is always fabricated
questions.explanation: Conversion factors (disability, age, environment, social norms) mean equal incomes yield unequal real freedoms, so income alone understates deprivation.

questions.q: Consumption expenditure is often preferred over income as a welfare measure in developing countries because:
options: Consumption is always higher than income
Consumption ignores food, simplifying calculations
Income is illegal to survey
Consumption is smoother, less volatile, and better reported by informal-sector households
questions.explanation: Households smooth consumption over time and report it more reliably than fluctuating informal-sector incomes, making it a steadier welfare proxy.

questions.q: The distinction between 'equity' and 'equality' is best captured by:
options: Equality means treating everyone the same; equity means allocating according to need to achieve fair outcomes
The two terms are exact synonyms
Equity means identical treatment; equality means fairness
Equity applies only to income; equality only to wealth
questions.explanation: Equality gives everyone the same, while equity distributes resources according to differing needs to produce fair outcomes.

questions.q: Proxy Means Testing (PMT) is a targeting method that:
options: Measures actual income directly through tax records
Selects beneficiaries by lottery
Targets entire geographic regions regardless of household status
Estimates welfare using observable proxies like assets and housing when income is hard to verify
questions.explanation: PMT predicts a household's welfare from easily observed characteristics (assets, education, housing) because direct income is unverifiable in informal economies.

questions.q: A recognized weakness of Proxy Means Testing is:
options: It always requires biometric identification
It can only be used in urban areas
Exclusion and inclusion errors arise because proxies imperfectly predict actual poverty
It is impossible to compute without census data
questions.explanation: Because proxies only approximate welfare, PMT wrongly excludes some genuinely poor households and includes some non-poor ones.

questions.q: 'Universal' provision (as opposed to targeted provision) of a benefit means:
options: It is means-tested annually
Everyone in a category receives it regardless of income
It is provided only to formal-sector workers
Only the poorest 10% receive it
questions.explanation: Universal schemes cover all members of a defined group (e.g., all children), avoiding targeting errors but at higher fiscal cost.

questions.q: Geographic (or 'area') targeting allocates benefits based on:
options: The poverty level of the region or locality where people live
The individual household's asset score
Self-declared income of applicants
Random selection within villages
questions.explanation: Geographic targeting directs resources to poor areas, which is administratively simple but misses poor households in richer regions.

questions.q: Self-targeting in welfare programs works by:
options: Assigning benefits by birth date
Designing benefits (e.g., manual labor for low wages) so only the genuinely needy choose to participate
Excluding anyone who applies voluntarily
Asking applicants to prove their income
questions.explanation: Self-targeting builds in conditions, like arduous work at low wages under MGNREGA, that make participation unattractive to the non-poor.

questions.q: India's MGNREGA is a classic example of which targeting mechanism?
options: Proxy means testing
Universal cash transfer
Self-targeting through a work requirement at a low statutory wage
Categorical targeting by caste alone
questions.explanation: MGNREGA offers manual work at a modest wage, so mainly those who need the income self-select into the program.

questions.q: The Foster–Greer–Thorbecke (FGT) class of poverty measures uses a parameter α such that when α = 0 the measure equals:
options: The headcount ratio
The Gini coefficient
The squared poverty gap
The poverty gap index
questions.explanation: In the FGT family, α = 0 gives the headcount ratio, α = 1 the poverty gap, and α = 2 the squared poverty gap (severity).

questions.q: In the FGT measures, setting α = 2 produces a measure that is especially sensitive to:
options: Inequality among the poor and the severity of deprivation
The number of rich households
The national mean income
The urban population share
questions.explanation: The squared poverty gap (α = 2) weights larger shortfalls more heavily, making it sensitive to inequality among the poor.

questions.q: An 'inclusion error' (leakage) in targeting occurs when:
options: Survey data is missing for a district
The poverty line is set too high
A non-poor household wrongly receives the benefit
A genuinely poor household is left out of the program
questions.explanation: Inclusion error (leakage) means benefits reach people who do not qualify, wasting resources meant for the poor.

questions.q: An 'exclusion error' (undercoverage) in targeting occurs when:
options: The program runs over budget
Two households receive the same benefit
An eligible poor household fails to receive the benefit
A non-poor household receives the benefit
questions.explanation: Exclusion error means genuinely eligible poor households are missed, undermining the program's poverty-reduction goal.

questions.q: The international extreme-poverty line most recently set by the World Bank (2022 update) is approximately:
options: $1.90 per day (2011 PPP)
$5.50 per day (2011 PPP)
$2.15 per day (2017 PPP)
$10.00 per day (2017 PPP)
questions.explanation: In 2022 the World Bank updated the international extreme-poverty line to $2.15 a day in 2017 purchasing-power-parity terms.

questions.q: The Palma ratio measures inequality as:
options: The income share of the top 10% divided by the share of the bottom 40%
The Gini divided by the poverty gap
The ratio of median to mean income
The top 1% share alone
questions.explanation: The Palma ratio compares the richest 10%'s income share to that of the poorest 40%, focusing on the tails of the distribution.

questions.q: A major advantage of the MPI over a purely monetary poverty measure is that it:
options: Reveals the specific deprivations (e.g., schooling, sanitation) that keep people poor
Requires no survey data
Always produces lower poverty counts
Ignores health to reduce complexity
questions.explanation: By decomposing poverty into indicators, the MPI shows which deprivations dominate, guiding sector-specific policy responses.

questions.q: Two Lorenz curves that cross each other imply that:
options: Gini rankings may disagree with other inequality measures, so ordering is ambiguous
The data must be erroneous
One distribution is unambiguously more equal than the other
Both distributions are perfectly equal
questions.explanation: When Lorenz curves intersect, no unambiguous inequality ranking exists and different indices can rank the distributions differently.

questions.q: The 'depth of poverty' is best captured by which measure?
options: Palma ratio
Poverty gap index
Gini coefficient
Headcount ratio
questions.explanation: The poverty gap index quantifies how far, on average, the poor fall below the line, i.e., the depth of poverty.

questions.q: The Sen poverty index is notable because it combines:
options: Income and wealth but not consumption
The headcount ratio, the poverty gap, and inequality among the poor (via a Gini term)
Health and education indicators
Only the headcount and the poverty line
questions.explanation: Sen's composite index integrates incidence (H), depth (poverty gap), and the distribution of income among the poor.

questions.q: Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) is used in cross-country poverty comparisons to:
options: Measure the depth of poverty within one country
Rank countries by GDP alone
Convert incomes at market exchange rates only
Adjust for differences in the cost of living so equal amounts buy comparable goods across countries
questions.explanation: PPP conversion accounts for price-level differences, making poverty lines comparable in real purchasing terms across countries.

questions.q: In the global MPI, the 'intensity' of poverty (A) refers to:
options: The poverty line value in dollars
The number of poor people
The average proportion of weighted deprivations experienced by those identified as poor
The rate of change in poverty over time
questions.explanation: Intensity A is the average share of weighted indicators in which multidimensionally poor people are deprived.

questions.q: A regressive tax system, in terms of equity, is one where:
options: The rich pay a higher share of income than the poor
Everyone pays the same absolute amount usefully
Only corporations are taxed
The poor pay a higher share of their income than the rich
questions.explanation: A regressive tax takes a larger proportion of income from low-income than high-income households, worsening after-tax inequality.

questions.q: Which statement about income versus consumption inequality in South Asia is generally accurate?
options: The two are always identical
Consumption inequality is typically lower than income inequality because households smooth consumption
Consumption inequality is usually higher than income inequality
Consumption inequality cannot be measured
questions.explanation: Because households save and borrow to smooth consumption, measured consumption inequality tends to be lower than income inequality.

questions.q: The NFHS in India collects data used for the MPI on standard-of-living indicators including:
options: Stock market participation
Cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, and assets
Foreign remittance flows only
Corporate tax filings
questions.explanation: NFHS captures household living-standard indicators (fuel, sanitation, water, electricity, housing, and assets) feeding the MPI's standard-of-living dimension.

questions.q: A poverty measure is said to satisfy the 'transfer axiom' if:
options: It stays constant when income moves between the poor
It ignores all income transfers
It rises when income is transferred from a poorer to a less-poor person
It only counts the number of poor
questions.explanation: The transfer (Pigou–Dalton) axiom requires the measure to worsen when a regressive transfer occurs among the poor; the headcount fails this axiom.

questions.q: The chief attraction of universal basic provision over targeted schemes is that it:
options: Costs less in total public spending
Guarantees only the poor benefit
Eliminates targeting errors and stigma, though at higher fiscal cost
Requires detailed asset surveys
questions.explanation: Universal provision avoids exclusion/inclusion errors and stigma but is fiscally costly since it covers non-poor recipients too.

questions.q: In India's PDS reform debate, the shift from 'targeted' (BPL/APL) to 'near-universal' coverage under the NFSA 2013 was motivated largely by:
options: Large exclusion errors in BPL identification leaving out many genuinely poor households
The elimination of all subsidies
A desire to reduce the number of beneficiaries
A switch to purely cash transfers
questions.explanation: Evidence of severe exclusion errors in BPL targeting drove the NFSA to cover roughly two-thirds of the population.

questions.q: The 'poverty severity index' (squared poverty gap) differs from the poverty gap index in that it:
options: Ignores the depth of poverty
Counts only the number of poor
Gives greater weight to the poorest among the poor
Equals the Gini coefficient
questions.explanation: By squaring the normalized gaps, the severity index places more weight on those furthest below the line, reflecting inequality among the poor.
