questions.q: A calorie-based (nutritional) poverty line in India historically used norms of approximately:
options: 1000 kcal urban and 800 kcal rural per day
3000 kcal for all areas
500 kcal per household
2100 kcal urban and 2400 kcal rural per person per day
questions.explanation: The original Indian poverty lines used calorie norms of 2100 kcal (urban) and 2400 kcal (rural) per capita per day.

questions.q: One reason MPI and monetary poverty estimates can diverge for the same population is that:
options: They always use the same households and give identical results
A household can be income-poor but not deprived in MPI indicators, or vice versa
MPI measures only income
Monetary poverty includes health and schooling
questions.explanation: Because they capture different aspects of deprivation, mismatch (income-poor but not MPI-poor, or the reverse) is common.

questions.q: The Kuznets curve hypothesizes that, as an economy develops, inequality:
options: Rises indefinitely without limit
First rises and then falls, forming an inverted-U
Remains perfectly constant
Falls continuously from the start
questions.explanation: Kuznets proposed an inverted-U: inequality increases in early development then declines as economies mature, an empirically contested pattern.

questions.q: A 'graduation' approach to poverty (e.g., BRAC's ultra-poor program in Bangladesh) primarily aims to:
options: Replace all state welfare with charity
Provide one-off cash and end support
Target only urban middle-class households
Sequence asset transfers, training, and support so households move sustainably out of extreme poverty
questions.explanation: Graduation programs combine asset transfers, coaching, savings, and consumption support to help the ultra-poor build sustainable livelihoods.

questions.q: When comparing two income distributions, if one Lorenz curve lies everywhere above (inside) another, it demonstrates:
options: Lorenz dominance: unambiguously lower inequality for the inner curve
Higher poverty for the inner curve
Ambiguous inequality ranking
Identical Gini coefficients
questions.explanation: A non-crossing Lorenz curve that lies closer to the equality line dominates, indicating unambiguously less inequality by all standard measures.

questions.q: Amartya Sen's 'capability approach' redefines development primarily as:
options: The expansion of people's real freedoms and capabilities to lead lives they value
Maximizing per-capita GDP growth
Accumulation of physical capital stock
Achieving a balanced trade surplus
questions.explanation: Sen argues development is best understood as expanding the substantive freedoms (capabilities) people have to achieve valued 'functionings', not merely income growth.

questions.q: In Sen's analysis of famines (e.g., Bengal 1943), the primary cause of starvation was:
options: An absolute shortage of food availability
A collapse in people's entitlements to acquire food, not just food supply
Deliberate government food destruction
Crop failure from drought alone
questions.explanation: Sen showed famines can occur without a fall in total food availability when groups lose their 'entitlements': the ability to command food through production, trade, or wages.

questions.q: A 'poverty trap' refers to a situation where:
options: Poverty is caused purely by individual laziness
Poverty automatically resolves as economies grow
Self-reinforcing mechanisms cause poverty to persist over time absent an external push
Only cultural factors keep people poor
questions.explanation: A poverty trap is a self-perpetuating condition, such as low nutrition limiting the ability to work, where being poor keeps people poor without an outside intervention.

questions.q: The 'S-shaped' capital-income relationship underlying poverty-trap models implies that:
options: The poor can always work their way out through small savings
Income grows linearly with capital at all levels
Aid is always counterproductive
Below a threshold of assets, people cannot accumulate enough to escape poverty
questions.explanation: In the S-curve model, those starting below a critical asset threshold end up poorer over time, while those above it grow richer: the geometric intuition behind poverty traps.

questions.q: Banerjee and Duflo, in 'Poor Economics', argue that anti-poverty policy should be guided primarily by:
options: Rigorous evidence on which specific interventions actually work, tested locally
Grand ideological theories about aid and markets
The intuitions of experienced bureaucrats
Maximizing aid volumes regardless of design
questions.explanation: Their central message is to move beyond the big 'aid vs. markets' debate and use experimental evidence to learn what concrete interventions improve poor people's lives.

questions.q: The 2019 Nobel Prize in Economics awarded to Banerjee, Duflo, and Kremer recognized their:
options: Theory of comparative advantage
Experimental approach to alleviating global poverty
Work on optimal currency areas
Model of endogenous growth
questions.explanation: The trio were honored for pioneering randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to test which development interventions effectively reduce poverty.

questions.q: A randomized controlled trial (RCT) identifies causal impact primarily because:
options: It uses the largest possible sample size
It relies on structural economic theory
Random assignment makes treatment and control groups statistically comparable on average
It surveys only the poorest households
questions.explanation: Randomization ensures that, on average, the treatment and control groups differ only in the intervention, so outcome differences can be attributed to the program.

questions.q: The 'counterfactual' in impact evaluation refers to:
options: A false claim made by program staff
The control group's demographic data
A hypothetical worst-case scenario
What would have happened to participants in the absence of the program
questions.explanation: Estimating impact requires comparing observed outcomes to the counterfactual: the outcome that would have occurred without the intervention.

questions.q: A conditional cash transfer (CCT) program provides money to households on the condition that they:
options: Meet specified behaviors such as school attendance or health check-ups
Repay the transfer with interest later
Purchase only government-approved goods
Belong to a particular political party
questions.explanation: CCTs like Mexico's Progresa/Oportunidades tie transfers to human-capital investments such as keeping children in school and attending clinics.

questions.q: Mexico's Progresa (later Oportunidades/Prospera) is notable in development economics because it was:
options: The first fully unconditional transfer program
Designed with a randomized rollout, enabling rigorous evaluation of a CCT
A microfinance-only scheme
An agricultural subsidy program
questions.explanation: Progresa's phased, randomized rollout allowed credible evaluation and helped popularize both CCTs and RCT-based evaluation worldwide.

questions.q: A key finding from comparisons of conditional vs. unconditional cash transfers is that:
options: Conditions never matter for any outcome
Unconditional transfers always outperform conditional ones on every metric
Conditions can boost targeted behaviors (e.g., schooling) but add administrative and enforcement costs
Cash transfers reliably increase spending on alcohol and tobacco
questions.explanation: Evidence suggests conditions can strengthen specific behaviors the condition targets, but they raise costs and exclude some needy households: the trade-off is context-dependent.

questions.q: A robust empirical finding across many cash-transfer studies is that recipients:
options: Typically waste transfers on 'temptation goods' like alcohol
Stop working entirely once they receive cash
Always save the entire amount
Do not, on average, increase spending on alcohol and tobacco
questions.explanation: Reviews (e.g., Evans and Popova) find little evidence that cash transfers systematically increase spending on alcohol or tobacco, countering a common objection.

questions.q: Muhammad Yunus and the Grameen Bank are most associated with pioneering:
options: Group-based microcredit for the poor, especially women
Conditional cash transfers
Sovereign wealth funds
Universal basic income
questions.explanation: Grameen Bank popularized joint-liability microcredit extending small collateral-free loans, primarily to poor women, and won the 2006 Nobel Peace Prize.

questions.q: Rigorous RCT evaluations of microcredit (e.g., Banerjee et al. 2015) generally found that microcredit:
options: Dramatically raised household incomes and lifted most borrowers out of poverty
Had modest effects, expanding some business activity but no transformative poverty reduction on average
Reliably empowered all women who received loans
Had strongly negative effects on all borrowers
questions.explanation: Multi-country RCTs found microcredit gave borrowers useful flexibility and some business investment, but no evidence of large average gains in income, consumption, or empowerment.

questions.q: The 'joint liability' feature of classic microfinance groups works by:
options: Having the government guarantee all loans
Requiring physical collateral from each borrower
Using peer pressure and shared responsibility so group members screen and monitor each other
Charging zero interest to all members
questions.explanation: Joint liability substitutes social collateral for physical collateral: group members have incentives to select trustworthy peers and ensure repayment.

questions.q: In Acemoglu and Robinson's 'Why Nations Fail', the fundamental driver of long-run prosperity is:
options: Geography and climate
Genetic or cultural traits of populations
The abundance of natural resources
Whether a country has inclusive rather than extractive political and economic institutions
questions.explanation: They argue inclusive institutions (broad property rights, checks on power, and open opportunity) foster growth, while extractive institutions concentrate power and stifle it.

questions.q: In the Acemoglu-Robinson framework, 'extractive' economic institutions are those that:
options: Are structured to extract resources from the many for the benefit of a narrow elite
Distribute opportunity and rewards broadly across society
Always coincide with democracy
Guarantee rapid industrialization
questions.explanation: Extractive institutions concentrate income and power in a small elite, providing little incentive for broad-based investment and innovation.

questions.q: Acemoglu, Johnson, and Robinson's 'settler mortality' study used disease environment as:
options: A direct cause of modern GDP
An instrumental variable to identify the causal effect of institutions on development
A measure of colonial population size
A proxy for natural-resource wealth
questions.explanation: They used historical settler mortality as an instrument for institutions, arguing high-mortality colonies got extractive institutions that persisted and depressed later development.

questions.q: Douglass North defined institutions as:
options: Only formal government agencies
Physical infrastructure like roads and ports
The 'rules of the game': humanly devised constraints that shape human interaction
International trade organizations
questions.explanation: North described institutions as the formal and informal rules structuring incentives in economic, political, and social exchange.

questions.q: 'Structural transformation' in development economics refers to:
options: The reshaping of a country's constitution
Privatization of state enterprises
The transition to a floating exchange rate
The shift of labor and output from agriculture toward industry and services
questions.explanation: Structural transformation is the reallocation of economic activity away from agriculture toward higher-productivity manufacturing and services as economies develop.

questions.q: The Lewis 'dual-sector' model describes development as driven by:
options: Labor moving from a low-productivity traditional (agricultural) sector to a modern (industrial) sector
Foreign aid inflows
Currency devaluation
Population control policies
questions.explanation: Arthur Lewis modeled growth as the transfer of 'surplus' labor from subsistence agriculture to the capitalist industrial sector, driving accumulation.

questions.q: India's growth path is often described as unusual because it featured:
options: Manufacturing-led growth like East Asia
A relatively large jump into services without a large manufacturing phase
No structural change at all
Growth driven entirely by oil exports
questions.explanation: India is frequently cited as skipping the classic manufacturing-led transition, with services (including IT) becoming a major growth engine: raising questions about job creation.

questions.q: Human capital, in development economics, primarily refers to:
options: The number of workers in a country
Machinery and equipment
The stock of knowledge, skills, and health embodied in people that raises productivity
Financial savings held by households
questions.explanation: Human capital is the productive capacity embodied in people via education, skills, and health, a central driver of long-run growth and earnings.

questions.q: A recurring RCT finding on education is that simply increasing school inputs (e.g., textbooks) often:
options: Always sharply raises test scores
Reduces enrollment
Only benefits the wealthiest students
Has limited average effects on learning unless teaching is targeted to children's actual level
questions.explanation: Studies (e.g., in Kenya and India's 'Teaching at the Right Level') show inputs alone often fail to raise learning; matching instruction to pupils' level is more effective.

questions.q: The 'Teaching at the Right Level' (TaRL) approach, evaluated with Pratham in India, works by:
options: Grouping children by current learning level rather than grade to target basic skills
Grouping children by age and covering the official curriculum faster
Paying students to attend school
Replacing teachers with technology
questions.explanation: TaRL reorganizes instruction around children's actual competency in reading and arithmetic rather than their grade, producing sizable learning gains in RCTs.

questions.q: Deworming programs became famous in development economics because RCTs suggested they:
options: Had no measurable effect on anything
Cheaply increased school attendance, with debated long-run economic benefits
Cured all childhood diseases
Only helped adults
questions.explanation: Miguel and Kremer's Kenya study found mass deworming cheaply raised school participation via reduced infection and spillovers, though magnitudes remain debated.

questions.q: The 'externality' rationale for subsidizing deworming or vaccination is that:
options: The benefits accrue only to the individual treated
Governments always know best
Treating one person reduces disease transmission, benefiting untreated others too
Private markets over-provide these goods
questions.explanation: Because treatment reduces contagion, it produces positive externalities that private decisions ignore, justifying public subsidy to reach the socially optimal level.

questions.q: William Easterly is best known for arguing that:
options: Aid should always be doubled
Institutions do not matter for growth
Central planning is the fastest route to development
Large top-down foreign aid 'plans' often fail; 'searchers' who adapt locally do better
questions.explanation: In 'The White Man's Burden', Easterly critiques grand aid 'planners' and champions accountable, feedback-driven 'searchers' who find workable local solutions.

questions.q: Jeffrey Sachs, in contrast to Easterly, has argued that:
options: A coordinated 'big push' of aid can help countries escape poverty traps
Aid is always harmful
Institutions are the only thing that matters
Markets alone will end extreme poverty
questions.explanation: Sachs contends that targeted, scaled-up aid investments (health, agriculture, infrastructure) can lift poor countries over poverty-trap thresholds: the 'big push' view.

questions.q: The 'micro-macro paradox' of aid (Mosley) refers to:
options: Aid being too small to measure
Aid working at the household level but showing weak effects on national growth
Micro and macro data being identical
Aid only helping macroeconomic stability
questions.explanation: The paradox is that many individual aid-funded projects appear successful, yet cross-country studies struggle to find a robust link between aid and aggregate growth.

questions.q: A key critique of relying on cross-country growth regressions to judge aid effectiveness is that:
options: They use too few variables
They are always experimental
Endogeneity and omitted variables make causal claims about aid and growth unreliable
They ignore GDP entirely
questions.explanation: Cross-country regressions suffer from reverse causality and confounding, so correlations between aid and growth are hard to interpret causally: a spur to RCT methods.

questions.q: 'Dutch disease' in the context of aid or resource booms refers to:
options: A public health epidemic
A form of corruption
Excessive borrowing from the IMF
Large inflows appreciating the real exchange rate and hurting export competitiveness
questions.explanation: Large aid or commodity inflows can raise the real exchange rate, making tradable sectors (like manufacturing) less competitive: the 'Dutch disease' effect.

questions.q: In the 'state vs. markets' debate, the East Asian 'developmental state' experience suggests that:
options: Active, capable states strategically guiding industrialization can accelerate development
Only laissez-faire markets produce growth
The state should own all firms
Trade should be fully closed
questions.explanation: Economies like South Korea and Taiwan combined markets with strong state coordination of industrial policy, credit, and exports to drive rapid catch-up growth.

questions.q: The 'Washington Consensus' set of policy prescriptions emphasized:
options: State ownership and central planning
Fiscal discipline, liberalization, privatization, and deregulation
Import-substitution industrialization
Universal basic income
questions.explanation: Coined by John Williamson, the Washington Consensus bundled market-oriented reforms (stabilization, liberalization, and privatization) promoted by Washington institutions in the 1990s.

questions.q: A common critique of the Washington Consensus is that it:
options: Was too focused on state-building
Recommended protectionism everywhere
Applied a one-size-fits-all template that neglected institutions and country context
Ignored fiscal policy entirely
questions.explanation: Critics like Rodrik and Stiglitz argue the standardized reform package underweighted institutions, sequencing, and context, yielding disappointing results in several regions.

questions.q: Dani Rodrik's 'growth diagnostics' approach recommends that reformers:
options: Apply the full reform checklist everywhere simultaneously
Rely solely on foreign advisors
Focus only on macroeconomic stability
Identify the most binding constraint on growth in a specific country and target it
questions.explanation: Growth diagnostics prioritizes finding and relaxing the single most binding constraint (e.g., finance, infrastructure, or institutions) rather than pursuing broad reforms at once.

questions.q: The 'resource curse' hypothesis holds that countries rich in natural resources often:
options: Tend to grow more slowly and suffer weaker institutions and volatility
Always grow faster than resource-poor countries
Have no exposure to global price swings
Automatically diversify their economies
questions.explanation: Resource abundance can be associated with slower growth, rent-seeking, conflict, and weak institutions: though outcomes depend heavily on governance quality.

questions.q: 'Import substitution industrialization' (ISI), pursued by India and Latin America mid-20th century, aimed to:
options: Maximize exports of primary commodities
Build domestic industry behind tariff protection to replace imported manufactures
Adopt free trade unilaterally
Attract only foreign direct investment
questions.explanation: ISI used tariffs and controls to nurture local industries producing goods previously imported, though it often produced inefficiency and was later criticized.

questions.q: Which statement best captures the 'external validity' concern with RCTs?
options: Results are never internally valid
RCTs cannot randomize
Findings from one context may not generalize to different settings or scales
RCTs always have small samples
questions.explanation: External validity questions whether a result found in a specific trial (place, population, implementer) holds elsewhere or when scaled up: a key limitation of RCTs.

questions.q: 'General equilibrium' effects that RCTs may miss include the possibility that:
options: The program has no cost
Participants always behave irrationally
Randomization fails
Scaling an intervention changes prices, wages, or markets in ways a small trial cannot detect
questions.explanation: A small RCT holds market-wide conditions fixed, but scaling up (e.g., a jobs or cash program) can shift wages or prices: general-equilibrium effects the trial cannot capture.

questions.q: The 'graduation' approach (BRAC, evaluated by Banerjee et al. 2015) for the ultra-poor combines:
options: A bundle: asset transfer, training, consumption support, coaching, and savings
Only a single cash grant
Microcredit loans alone
Only school subsidies
questions.explanation: The multi-faceted 'graduation' model layers a productive asset, temporary consumption support, training, and coaching, and showed lasting gains across six-country RCTs.

questions.q: Esther Duflo's work on women in local government (India's panchayat reservations) found that female leaders:
options: Made no difference to policy
Shifted public-goods investment toward priorities like water, and affected girls' aspirations
Reduced overall development spending
Were universally rejected by voters
questions.explanation: Studies of India's gender quotas found reserved female-led councils invested more in infrastructure women prioritized and raised aspirations and educational outcomes for girls.

questions.q: The concept of 'missing markets' for the poor (e.g., credit, insurance) matters because:
options: The poor never want to save
Markets always function perfectly
Absent credit or insurance, the poor cannot make profitable investments or manage risk efficiently
Only governments face risk
questions.explanation: Imperfect or missing credit and insurance markets prevent poor households from investing optimally and force costly risk-coping, a core theme in Banerjee-Duflo's work.

questions.q: 'Nudges' and behavioral insights in development (e.g., small incentives for immunization) reflect the idea that:
options: The poor are fundamentally irrational
Only large cash grants change behavior
Information never matters
Small frictions and defaults strongly shape behavior, so modest design changes can have outsized effects
questions.explanation: Behavioral development economics shows that reducing small hassles or adding modest incentives (like lentils for vaccination) can substantially raise take-up of beneficial services.

questions.q: The Millennium Villages Project drew criticism mainly because it:
options: Lacked a credible comparison group, making its claimed impacts hard to attribute
Used a rigorous randomized design
Was too small to matter
Focused only on urban areas
questions.explanation: Critics argued the integrated 'big push' project lacked proper counterfactual comparison villages, so improvements could not be reliably attributed to the intervention.

questions.q: A universal basic income (UBI) differs from a conditional cash transfer chiefly in that UBI is:
options: Paid only to employed workers
Unconditional and typically universal, with no behavioral requirements or means test
Always larger in amount
Restricted to health spending
questions.explanation: UBI provides regular payments to all (or a broad population) without conditions or means-testing, contrasting with CCTs' targeted, behavior-linked design.

questions.q: The main argument for cash transfers over in-kind aid is that:
options: Cash is always cheaper to steal
In-kind aid can never be justified
Cash gives recipients flexibility to meet their own priorities, often more efficiently
Recipients cannot be trusted with cash
questions.explanation: Cash respects recipients' knowledge of their own needs and avoids the logistical costs and mismatches of in-kind distribution, though in-kind can suit specific goals.

questions.q: Kremer's 'O-ring' theory of development suggests that:
options: Production is unaffected by worker quality
Only capital matters for output
Low-skill economies always catch up quickly
Because tasks are complementary, small quality failures can sharply reduce output, favoring skill clustering
questions.explanation: The O-ring model (named after the Challenger disaster) shows that when tasks must all be done well, mistakes are costly and high-skill workers cluster together, amplifying inequality across firms and nations.

questions.q: In development economics, 'convergence' (in the neoclassical growth sense) predicts that:
options: Poorer economies should grow faster and catch up to richer ones, all else equal
Rich and poor countries permanently diverge
All countries grow at identical rates
Growth is impossible without aid
questions.explanation: The Solow model predicts conditional convergence, poorer countries with similar fundamentals grow faster due to higher returns to capital, though unconditional convergence is weak in the data.

questions.q: A central lesson practitioners draw from the RCT 'evidence movement' is to:
options: Abandon all theory and economics
Pilot and rigorously test interventions before scaling, and remain humble about what works
Trust only anecdotes from the field
Adopt any policy proven to work in a rich country
questions.explanation: The evidence movement urges testing programs with credible evaluation and scaling those shown to work, while recognizing context-dependence and the limits of generalization.

questions.q: In public finance, what is the primary distinction between direct and indirect taxes?
options: Direct taxes are levied by the central government while indirect taxes are levied by states
Direct taxes are paid directly by the person on whom they are legally imposed, whereas the burden of indirect taxes can be shifted to others
Direct taxes apply only to income while indirect taxes apply only to wealth
Direct taxes are collected annually while indirect taxes are collected monthly
questions.explanation: A direct tax (like income tax) is borne by the person legally liable, while an indirect tax (like GST) is levied on goods/services and its burden can be passed on to the final consumer.

questions.q: A tax where the average tax rate rises as income increases is described as:
options: Regressive
Proportional
Lump-sum
Progressive
questions.explanation: A progressive tax takes a larger percentage of income as income rises, so the average rate increases with income.

questions.q: A tax that takes a larger share of income from low-income households than from high-income households is:
options: Progressive
Proportional
Marginal
Regressive
questions.explanation: A regressive tax burdens the poor proportionally more, as commonly happens with consumption taxes on essentials.

questions.q: Why are broad-based consumption taxes like GST often considered regressive in their impact?
options: Because rich households pay a higher rate on the same goods
Because they are collected only from formal-sector workers
Because they exempt luxury goods entirely
Because poorer households spend a larger proportion of their income on taxed consumption
questions.explanation: Since lower-income households consume (rather than save) most of their income, a flat consumption tax claims a larger share of their income.

questions.q: The Goods and Services Tax (GST) is best classified as a:
options: Destination-based indirect tax on consumption
Direct tax on income
Origin-based tax on production
Wealth tax on assets
questions.explanation: GST is a destination-based, value-added indirect tax levied on the consumption of goods and services, with revenue accruing where consumption occurs.

questions.q: Under India's dual GST structure, a transaction within a single state attracts:
options: Only IGST
CGST and SGST together
Only a state VAT
CGST and IGST together
questions.explanation: Intra-state supplies attract Central GST (CGST) and State GST (SGST) simultaneously, splitting revenue between the centre and the state.

questions.q: In India's GST framework, IGST (Integrated GST) applies to:
options: Only exports
Only luxury goods
Inter-state supplies of goods and services
Local municipal transactions
questions.explanation: IGST is levied on inter-state supplies and imports, and is later apportioned between the centre and the destination state.

questions.q: A key advantage of the value-added tax (VAT) design underlying GST is that it:
options: Taxes the full value at every stage without any credit, maximizing revenue
Allows input tax credit so tax is effectively paid only on value added at each stage
Applies only at the retail stage
Eliminates the need for any record-keeping
questions.explanation: The input tax credit mechanism means each business is taxed only on the value it adds, avoiding the cascading of tax on tax.

questions.q: The 'cascading effect' of taxation that GST was designed to eliminate refers to:
options: Multiple states charging the same rate
Taxes being levied on tax already paid at earlier stages, i.e., tax-on-tax
Progressive rate slabs stacking up
Taxes cascading down to consumers only
questions.explanation: Cascading occurs when tax is charged on a base that already includes tax from prior stages; input credits under GST break this chain.

questions.q: The fiscal deficit of a government is best defined as:
options: The excess of total expenditure over total revenue receipts and non-debt capital receipts (i.e., total borrowing)
Total expenditure minus total revenue including borrowings
Revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts
Interest payments minus tax revenue
questions.explanation: The fiscal deficit equals total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings, so it measures the government's total borrowing requirement.

questions.q: The revenue deficit specifically measures:
options: The shortfall of capital receipts over capital expenditure
Total borrowing minus interest payments
The gap between planned and actual spending
The excess of revenue expenditure over revenue receipts
questions.explanation: Revenue deficit is the excess of the government's revenue (current) expenditure over its revenue receipts, indicating dis-saving.

questions.q: The primary deficit is calculated as:
options: Fiscal deficit plus interest payments
Fiscal deficit minus interest payments
Revenue deficit minus interest receipts
Fiscal deficit minus revenue deficit
questions.explanation: The primary deficit is the fiscal deficit less interest payments, showing borrowing needs excluding the legacy cost of past debt.

questions.q: A country running a persistent primary deficit of zero but a large fiscal deficit indicates that:
options: Its current borrowing is driven mainly by interest payments on accumulated past debt
It has no debt at all
Its revenue exceeds all expenditure
It is repaying debt rapidly
questions.explanation: If the primary deficit is zero, the entire fiscal deficit is attributable to interest on existing debt, signalling a debt-servicing burden.

questions.q: Public debt sustainability is generally more assured when:
options: The nominal interest rate on debt exceeds the growth rate of GDP
The government never runs a primary surplus
Debt is entirely denominated in foreign currency
The growth rate of GDP exceeds the effective interest rate on debt, and primary balances are managed
questions.explanation: When GDP growth outpaces the interest rate on debt, the debt-to-GDP ratio tends to fall or stabilize even with modest deficits.

questions.q: The debt-to-GDP ratio is a preferred measure of a country's debt burden because it:
options: Ignores the size of the economy
Measures only annual borrowing
Counts only external debt
Relates the stock of debt to the economy's capacity to service it
questions.explanation: Scaling debt by GDP shows the burden relative to the nation's income and ability to repay, allowing cross-country and over-time comparison.

questions.q: 'Crowding out' in public finance refers to the phenomenon where:
options: Government spending attracts more private investment
Foreign investors leave the country
Heavy government borrowing raises interest rates and reduces private investment
Taxes crowd out consumption of luxury goods
questions.explanation: When the government borrows heavily, it can push up interest rates and absorb loanable funds, discouraging private sector borrowing and investment.

questions.q: Tax incidence analysis is primarily concerned with:
options: Who is legally required to pay a tax
How often a tax is collected
Who ultimately bears the economic burden of a tax after price adjustments
Which agency administers the tax
questions.explanation: Tax incidence studies the final distribution of the tax burden, which may differ from statutory liability due to shifting through prices.

questions.q: The economic burden of a tax on a good tends to fall more heavily on consumers when:
options: Demand is relatively inelastic relative to supply
Demand is highly elastic relative to supply
The good is a perfect substitute for many others
Supply is perfectly elastic and demand is elastic
questions.explanation: When demand is inelastic (consumers cannot easily reduce purchases), sellers can pass more of the tax onto consumers via higher prices.

questions.q: The 'deadweight loss' of a tax refers to:
options: The revenue lost to tax evasion
The administrative cost of collecting the tax
The interest cost on public debt
The loss of economic efficiency (foregone mutually beneficial trades) caused by the tax distorting behaviour
questions.explanation: Deadweight loss is the reduction in total surplus from transactions that no longer occur because the tax drives a wedge between prices.

questions.q: A subsidy is best described in public finance terms as:
options: A government payment or benefit that reduces the price paid by consumers or the cost borne by producers
A tax levied on producers
A loan repayable with interest
A transfer only to government employees
questions.explanation: A subsidy is a form of government support that lowers costs/prices to promote consumption or production of a good or service.

questions.q: In South Asian welfare policy, 'targeting' of subsidies refers to:
options: Setting revenue targets for tax authorities
Meeting fiscal deficit targets
Aiming subsidies at exporters
Directing benefits specifically to intended (usually poorer) beneficiaries rather than everyone
questions.explanation: Targeting seeks to channel subsidies to those who need them most, improving efficiency and reducing leakage to the non-poor.

questions.q: A 'universal' subsidy differs from a 'targeted' subsidy in that it:
options: Only reaches the poorest 10 percent
Requires biometric authentication
Is available to all eligible consumers regardless of income
Is funded entirely by external donors
questions.explanation: Universal subsidies apply to everyone consuming the good, whereas targeted subsidies restrict eligibility, typically by income or other criteria.

questions.q: An 'inclusion error' in subsidy targeting occurs when:
options: A deserving poor household is wrongly excluded from benefits
A non-poor household wrongly receives benefits intended for the poor
The subsidy budget is exhausted early
The subsidy is paid in cash rather than in kind
questions.explanation: Inclusion (Type II) error means benefits leak to those who should not receive them, wasting resources on the non-target group.

questions.q: An 'exclusion error' in a targeted welfare programme refers to:
options: Genuinely eligible poor people being left out of the programme
Ineligible people receiving benefits
The programme excluding luxury goods
Excluding foreign nationals
questions.explanation: Exclusion (Type I) error occurs when intended beneficiaries are wrongly denied benefits, undermining the programme's welfare goals.

questions.q: Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) schemes in India aim primarily to:
options: Increase indirect tax collection
Reduce leakage and intermediary diversion by transferring subsidies directly to beneficiaries' bank accounts
Replace all taxes with transfers
Eliminate the need for a budget
questions.explanation: DBT routes subsidy payments directly to beneficiaries (often via Aadhaar-linked accounts) to cut leakage, ghost beneficiaries, and middlemen.

questions.q: The main efficiency argument for replacing in-kind subsidies with cash transfers is that cash:
options: Is easier to divert than food grains
Guarantees the good is consumed only by children
Preserves consumer choice and reduces storage/distribution costs and leakage
Automatically indexes to inflation
questions.explanation: Cash transfers let recipients choose how to spend, avoid costly physical distribution, and can reduce diversion, though they may lose the earmarking of in-kind support.

questions.q: Government revenue receipts are typically divided into:
options: Tax revenue and non-tax revenue
Capital receipts and borrowings
Grants and loans only
Direct and progressive receipts
questions.explanation: Revenue receipts comprise tax revenue (income tax, GST, etc.) and non-tax revenue (fees, dividends, interest, royalties).

questions.q: Which of the following is a capital receipt rather than a revenue receipt for a government?
options: Proceeds from disinvestment of a public sector enterprise
Income tax collections
GST collections
Interest received on loans given
questions.explanation: Disinvestment proceeds reduce government assets and are a capital receipt, unlike recurring tax or interest income which are revenue receipts.

questions.q: Capital expenditure by a government is best characterized as spending that:
options: Is used for salaries and interest payments
Recurs every month regardless of outcomes
Creates assets or reduces liabilities, such as building infrastructure
Only covers subsidies
questions.explanation: Capital expenditure creates physical or financial assets (roads, buildings) or repays debt, unlike revenue expenditure which is for day-to-day running.

questions.q: Interest payments on government debt are classified in the budget as:
options: Capital expenditure
A capital receipt
Revenue (current) expenditure
A subsidy
questions.explanation: Interest payments do not create assets; they are recurring revenue expenditure and often a large component of it.

questions.q: Intergovernmental fiscal transfers refer to:
options: Transfers of tax money between two private firms
Foreign aid between two countries
The flow of funds from one level of government (e.g., central) to another (e.g., state/local)
Transfers within a single ministry
questions.explanation: Intergovernmental transfers move resources across tiers of government to address vertical and horizontal fiscal imbalances.

questions.q: In India, the body that recommends the formula for sharing central taxes with states is the:
options: Finance Commission
Reserve Bank of India
Securities and Exchange Board
Planning Commission (now NITI Aayog)
questions.explanation: The Finance Commission, a constitutional body constituted periodically, recommends the vertical and horizontal devolution of central tax revenues to states.

questions.q: 'Vertical fiscal imbalance' in a federation refers to a mismatch between:
options: The revenue-raising powers and expenditure responsibilities across different levels of government
Two states of similar size
Tax rates in urban versus rural areas
Central and foreign governments
questions.explanation: Vertical imbalance arises when a level of government (often sub-national) has larger spending duties than its own revenue capacity, requiring transfers.

questions.q: 'Horizontal fiscal equalization' transfers are designed to:
options: Reduce disparities in fiscal capacity among governments at the same level (e.g., across states)
Move funds from the centre to itself
Equalize interest rates across banks
Balance revenue and capital budgets
questions.explanation: Horizontal equalization channels more resources to poorer regions so that comparable public services can be provided across states with unequal capacity.

questions.q: 'Conditional' (tied) grants to sub-national governments differ from 'unconditional' (untied) grants because conditional grants:
options: Can be spent on anything the recipient chooses
Must be used for specified purposes set by the grantor
Never require any reporting
Are always larger in amount
questions.explanation: Conditional grants earmark funds for particular programmes or sectors, whereas unconditional grants can be used at the recipient's discretion.

questions.q: The principle of 'fiscal federalism' concerns:
options: Only the taxation of foreign firms
The division of taxing, spending, and borrowing functions among different levels of government
The federal reserve's monetary policy
The merger of state budgets into one national budget
questions.explanation: Fiscal federalism studies how fiscal responsibilities and resources are best assigned across national, regional, and local governments.

questions.q: A 'balanced budget' occurs when:
options: Revenue receipts exactly equal total expenditure
Capital expenditure equals revenue expenditure
Tax revenue equals subsidy spending
Total government receipts equal total government expenditure
questions.explanation: A balanced budget means total receipts match total expenditure so there is no overall deficit or surplus.

questions.q: Automatic stabilizers in public finance are:
options: Discretionary stimulus packages passed each year
Fixed interest rates set by the central bank
Features like progressive taxes and unemployment benefits that dampen the business cycle without new legislation
One-time capital grants to states
questions.explanation: Automatic stabilizers adjust automatically, tax take falls and transfers rise in downturns, cushioning demand without new policy action.

questions.q: The 'ability-to-pay' principle of taxation holds that:
options: Taxes should be based on the benefits each person receives from public services
Everyone should pay an identical lump-sum amount
Only property owners should be taxed
Those with greater economic capacity should pay more tax
questions.explanation: The ability-to-pay principle justifies progressive taxation by linking tax liability to a taxpayer's capacity to bear the burden.

questions.q: The 'benefit principle' of taxation suggests that:
options: The rich should always pay the highest rate
Taxes should be levied in proportion to the benefits taxpayers receive from public goods
Taxes should fund only defence
Taxes should never fund public services
questions.explanation: The benefit principle links tax payments to the benefits received, as with user charges or earmarked road taxes funding highways.

questions.q: Public goods such as national defence are difficult to fund through markets mainly because they are:
options: Rival and excludable
Non-rival and non-excludable, leading to free-rider problems
Always produced by private firms efficiently
Subject to high import duties
questions.explanation: Non-excludability lets people benefit without paying (free riding), so public goods are typically financed through taxation.

questions.q: A 'tax expenditure' refers to:
options: Government spending on tax collection staff
Money spent on printing tax forms
Revenue foregone through exemptions, deductions, and concessions in the tax code
The administrative budget of the tax department
questions.explanation: Tax expenditures are the revenue the government forgoes via preferential provisions, functionally equivalent to direct spending on those beneficiaries.

questions.q: The Laffer curve illustrates the idea that:
options: Higher tax rates always raise more revenue
Tax revenue is independent of the tax rate
Beyond a certain point, raising tax rates can reduce total tax revenue
Lower rates always reduce revenue proportionally
questions.explanation: The Laffer curve posits that very high rates can discourage activity or encourage evasion so that revenue falls, implying a revenue-maximizing rate.

questions.q: 'Tax buoyancy' measures:
options: How responsive tax revenue is to changes in GDP, including effects of rate and base changes
The physical weight of tax documents
The interest earned on tax deposits
The number of taxpayers in a country
questions.explanation: Tax buoyancy captures the percentage change in tax revenue relative to the percentage change in GDP, reflecting overall revenue responsiveness.

questions.q: A large 'informal economy' in South Asia constrains direct tax collection primarily because:
options: Informal workers pay very high income tax
Informal firms overpay GST
Much income and many transactions are unrecorded and outside the tax net
Informality increases corporate tax compliance
questions.explanation: A big informal sector means many earnings escape documentation, narrowing the direct tax base and shifting reliance toward indirect taxes.

questions.q: The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act in India was enacted to:
options: Increase subsidies without limit
Abolish the Finance Commission
Fix all commodity prices
Institutionalize fiscal discipline by setting targets for deficits and debt
questions.explanation: The FRBM Act aims to reduce fiscal and revenue deficits and cap debt, promoting macroeconomic stability and transparency in fiscal management.

questions.q: A 'countercyclical' fiscal policy during a recession would typically involve:
options: Cutting spending and raising taxes to balance the budget
Increasing spending and/or cutting taxes to stimulate demand
Keeping the budget exactly balanced regardless of conditions
Only raising indirect taxes
questions.explanation: Countercyclical policy expands the deficit in downturns (more spending, lower taxes) to support aggregate demand and employment.

questions.q: In a progressive income tax with slabs, the 'marginal tax rate' is:
options: The average rate across all income
The rate applied to the last (additional) unit of income earned
A flat rate on total income
The rate on capital gains only
questions.explanation: The marginal rate applies to the next rupee of income in the highest slab reached, and it exceeds the average rate under progressivity.

questions.q: A specific 'sin tax' (e.g., on tobacco or alcohol) is justified in public finance mainly as a way to:
options: Subsidize consumption of the good
Reward heavy users
Reduce government revenue deliberately
Correct a negative externality and discourage harmful consumption while raising revenue
questions.explanation: Sin taxes internalize the social costs (health, externalities) of harmful goods, reducing consumption while generating revenue: a Pigouvian rationale.

questions.q: When evaluating a subsidy programme, 'leakage' most precisely refers to:
options: The share of intended benefits that fails to reach target beneficiaries due to diversion or errors
Water lost from public infrastructure
The delay in disbursing funds
The interest cost of financing the subsidy
questions.explanation: Leakage is the portion of subsidy value lost to corruption, ghost beneficiaries, or mistargeting, reducing the programme's effective reach to the poor.

questions.q: In the classic policy cycle model, which stage involves defining which problems get onto the government's list of priorities for action?
options: Agenda-setting
Policy formulation
Policy adoption
Policy evaluation
questions.explanation: Agenda-setting is the stage where issues compete for attention and a subset is recognised as problems warranting government action.

questions.q: What is the conventional sequence of stages in the standard policy cycle?
options: Formulation, agenda-setting, adoption, evaluation, implementation
Agenda-setting, formulation, adoption, implementation, evaluation
Adoption, formulation, implementation, agenda-setting, evaluation
Implementation, adoption, evaluation, formulation, agenda-setting
questions.explanation: The heuristic cycle runs agenda-setting to formulation to adoption to implementation to evaluation, often feeding back into the agenda.

questions.q: In John Kingdon's Multiple Streams Framework, the three streams that must converge to open a policy window are the problem stream, the policy stream, and which third stream?
options: The financial stream
The bureaucratic stream
The politics stream
The media stream
questions.explanation: Kingdon identifies the problem, policy (solutions), and politics streams, whose coupling at a policy window enables agenda change.

questions.q: Kingdon's term for individuals who invest resources to couple problems, solutions, and politics when a window opens is:
options: Street-level bureaucrats
Veto players
Epistemic communities
Policy entrepreneurs
questions.explanation: Policy entrepreneurs seize open windows by joining the streams and advocating their preferred solution.

questions.q: In the Multiple Streams Framework, a 'policy window' is best described as:
options: A fixed annual budget deadline
A permanent institutional venue for debate
A fleeting opportunity for advocates to push their solutions onto the agenda
The legal period for public consultation
questions.explanation: Policy windows are transient openings, often triggered by events or political change, during which coupling of the streams can succeed.

questions.q: The Overton window refers to:
options: The range of policies the public will accept as politically legitimate at a given time
A budget ceiling set by the finance ministry
The period a bill can be amended in parliament
The margin of error in a policy forecast
questions.explanation: The Overton window describes the spectrum of ideas considered acceptable to mainstream public opinion, which can shift over time.

questions.q: Shifting the Overton window typically means:
options: Reducing the number of policy options considered
Accelerating the legislative timetable
Increasing the discount rate in appraisal
Changing what society regards as politically thinkable or acceptable
questions.explanation: Advocates 'move the window' by making previously radical ideas seem mainstream, expanding the range of acceptable policy.

questions.q: Evidence-based policy is best defined as an approach that:
options: Relies solely on expert intuition
Uses rigorous research and data to inform policy decisions
Bases decisions only on public opinion polls
Follows historical precedent without review
questions.explanation: Evidence-based policy explicitly grounds choices in the best available research evidence alongside other considerations.

questions.q: A commonly cited limitation of a strict 'evidence-based policy' ideal is that:
options: Evidence is never generated by researchers
Policy is shaped by values, politics and context, not evidence alone
Randomised trials are illegal in most countries
Evidence always points to one clear answer
questions.explanation: Critics note that political feasibility, values and context mediate how, and whether, evidence is used, hence 'evidence-informed' is often preferred.

questions.q: Cost-benefit analysis (CBA) evaluates a policy by:
options: Comparing outcomes only in physical units
Monetising and comparing all costs and benefits
Ranking options by public popularity
Measuring only the upfront capital cost
questions.explanation: CBA expresses both costs and benefits in monetary terms to judge whether net benefits are positive.

questions.q: Cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA) differs from cost-benefit analysis mainly because CEA:
options: Monetises benefits as well as costs
Measures outcomes in natural units (e.g., lives saved) rather than money
Ignores costs entirely
Applies only to private-sector projects
questions.explanation: CEA keeps benefits in physical/natural units such as cost per life saved, avoiding the need to place a money value on outcomes.

questions.q: In cost-benefit analysis, discounting is used to:
options: Adjust future costs and benefits to present value
Remove low-income beneficiaries from the calculation
Increase the nominal size of benefits
Convert foreign currency to local currency
questions.explanation: Discounting converts streams of future costs and benefits into comparable present-value terms.

questions.q: The net present value (NPV) decision rule generally recommends accepting a project when:
options: NPV is negative
NPV equals zero exactly
The discount rate exceeds the interest rate
NPV is positive
questions.explanation: A positive NPV indicates discounted benefits exceed discounted costs, signalling a worthwhile investment.

questions.q: A cost-effectiveness ratio is typically expressed as:
options: Total benefits minus total costs
Cost per unit of outcome achieved
The ratio of two monetary benefit streams
Benefits divided by the discount rate
questions.explanation: CEA reports cost per unit of effect, e.g., cost per DALY averted or per child immunised, enabling comparison across options.

questions.q: Policy instruments are best understood as:
options: The measurable indicators used in evaluation
The tools or means governments use to achieve policy goals
The committees that draft legislation
The agencies that lobby government
questions.explanation: Instruments (regulation, taxes, subsidies, information, direct provision) are the mechanisms through which policy objectives are pursued.

questions.q: A subsidy for solar panels is an example of which broad category of policy instrument?
options: Regulatory (command-and-control)
Economic/fiscal (incentive-based)
Information/persuasion
Direct government provision
questions.explanation: Subsidies work through financial incentives, a hallmark of economic or market-based instruments.

questions.q: A public awareness campaign encouraging handwashing is which type of policy instrument?
options: Information/suasion
Taxation
Regulation
Nationalisation
questions.explanation: Awareness campaigns rely on information and persuasion (nodality) rather than legal compulsion or financial incentives.

questions.q: In Hood's classic 'NATO' typology, the four categories of government resource for policy tools are Nodality, Authority, Treasure, and:
options: Technology
Territory
Timing
Organisation
questions.explanation: Hood's NATO scheme classifies instruments by the government resource used: Nodality (information), Authority, Treasure (money), and Organisation.

questions.q: The 'implementation gap' refers to:
options: The delay between drafting and printing a law
The difference between a policy's stated goals and what is actually delivered
The funding shortfall in a national budget
The time lag before evaluation begins
questions.explanation: The implementation gap is the divergence between intended policy outcomes and on-the-ground results during delivery.

questions.q: Pressman and Wildavsky's classic study of implementation famously highlighted that:
options: Implementation is automatic once a law is passed
Multiple actors and decision points ('the complexity of joint action') can derail even agreed policies
Only funding determines success
Evaluation should precede formulation
questions.explanation: Their Oakland study showed that many required agreements and clearance points compound to frustrate implementation.

questions.q: Michael Lipsky's concept of 'street-level bureaucrats' emphasises that:
options: Senior ministers control every service delivery detail
Frontline workers exercise discretion that effectively shapes policy as delivered
Policy is implemented identically everywhere
Bureaucrats have no influence on outcomes
questions.explanation: Street-level bureaucrats (teachers, nurses, caseworkers) use discretion under pressure, in effect making policy at the point of delivery.

questions.q: A 'top-down' approach to implementation research assumes that:
options: Frontline discretion is the main driver of outcomes
Implementation flows from clear central goals cascaded down through the hierarchy
Local networks negotiate policy from the bottom up
Policy goals are irrelevant to delivery
questions.explanation: Top-down models start from authoritative central decisions and assess how faithfully they are carried out down the chain.

questions.q: A 'bottom-up' approach to implementation stresses that:
options: Only statutory objectives matter
Central control guarantees success
Evaluation is unnecessary
Understanding delivery requires starting from frontline actors and local networks
questions.explanation: Bottom-up analysts begin with the actors closest to the problem, arguing their behaviour and networks determine real outcomes.

questions.q: Stakeholder analysis in policy is primarily used to:
options: Calculate the discount rate
Identify actors affected by or able to affect a policy, and their interests and influence
Set the tax rate
Draft the final legislation
questions.explanation: Stakeholder analysis maps who has a stake, their positions, power and interests, to inform strategy and feasibility.

questions.q: A power-interest grid in stakeholder analysis classifies stakeholders by their level of power and their:
options: Geographic location
Level of interest in the issue
Annual income
Political party affiliation
questions.explanation: The grid plots power against interest, guiding whether to manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, or monitor each actor.

questions.q: In a power-interest matrix, stakeholders with high power and high interest should typically be:
options: Ignored
Monitored with minimal effort
Managed closely and engaged actively
Kept informed only occasionally
questions.explanation: High-power, high-interest actors are 'key players' who should be managed closely because they can strongly shape outcomes.

questions.q: The problem stream in Kingdon's framework becomes prominent through which of the following?
options: Indicators, focusing events, and feedback
Only the personal preferences of ministers
The size of the national debt alone
Election dates exclusively
questions.explanation: Problems rise via changes in indicators, dramatic focusing events, and feedback showing existing programmes are failing.

questions.q: A sudden disaster that dramatically raises attention to a problem and can open a policy window is called a:
options: Sunset clause
Veto point
Policy legacy
Focusing event
questions.explanation: Focusing events (crises, disasters, crises) concentrate public and political attention, often opening windows for action.

questions.q: 'Softening up' in the policy stream refers to:
options: Reducing a programme's budget
Gradually building acceptance of ideas among specialists and the public over time
Weakening enforcement of a law
Lowering the discount rate
questions.explanation: Kingdon describes 'softening up' as the process by which proposals gain acceptance through repeated exposure and debate.

questions.q: Which of the following is a limitation of using cost-benefit analysis for social policy?
options: It cannot handle any monetary values
Placing money values on intangibles like life, health or environment is contentious
It ignores costs completely
It always favours the poorest groups
questions.explanation: CBA requires monetising hard-to-value outcomes, raising ethical and technical objections, especially for equity-sensitive policy.

questions.q: Distributional (equity) analysis is added to cost-benefit analysis mainly to address the fact that standard CBA:
options: Overstates all costs
Focuses on aggregate efficiency and can ignore who gains and who loses
Cannot be quantified
Only applies to health projects
questions.explanation: Because CBA sums net benefits, it may mask distributional impacts; equity weighting or analysis reveals who bears costs and benefits.

questions.q: In South Asia, a frequently cited cause of implementation gaps in social programmes is:
options: Excessive frontline autonomy with no rules
Weak administrative capacity, leakage, and coordination failures across tiers of government
Complete absence of any policy
Over-funding of every scheme
questions.explanation: Capacity constraints, leakage/corruption, and poor inter-agency and centre-state coordination commonly widen the gap between design and delivery.

questions.q: Policy evaluation that assesses whether a programme caused its intended outcomes is known as:
options: Process evaluation
Impact evaluation
Formative evaluation
Needs assessment
questions.explanation: Impact evaluation seeks to establish causal attribution: the change attributable to the intervention itself.

questions.q: Process (or implementation) evaluation primarily examines:
options: Whether the intended long-term impact occurred
The monetary value of benefits
The political feasibility of adoption
How a programme is delivered, its fidelity, reach and operations
questions.explanation: Process evaluation looks at how well a programme is being implemented (coverage, quality, fidelity) rather than ultimate impact.

questions.q: A counterfactual in impact evaluation represents:
options: The programme's budget forecast
What would have happened to beneficiaries in the absence of the programme
The stakeholders opposed to the policy
The upper bound of costs
questions.explanation: The counterfactual is the estimated outcome without the intervention, the benchmark against which impact is measured.

questions.q: The 'garbage can' model of decision-making, related to Kingdon's work, portrays organisations as places where:
options: Decisions follow a strictly rational sequence
Problems, solutions and choice opportunities are mixed somewhat chaotically
Only budgets determine outcomes
Frontline workers have no role
questions.explanation: Cohen, March and Olsen's garbage can model sees choices emerging from a loose mix of problems, solutions and participants.

questions.q: Incrementalism, associated with Charles Lindblom's 'muddling through', describes policy-making as:
options: Comprehensive rational analysis of all options
Small, marginal adjustments to existing policy
Random selection of policies
Complete overhaul at each cycle
questions.explanation: Lindblom argued that in practice policymakers make limited, incremental changes rather than fully rational comprehensive decisions.

questions.q: The 'rational-comprehensive' model of policy analysis is often criticised because:
options: It requires too little information
Real decision-makers face bounded rationality, limited time, and incomplete information
It never sets objectives
It only applies to evaluation
questions.explanation: Critics note humans and institutions cannot gather and weigh all information; bounded rationality limits the ideal-rational approach.

questions.q: Herbert Simon's concept of 'satisficing' means decision-makers tend to:
options: Optimise across every possible option
Choose the first option that is 'good enough' rather than optimal
Avoid making any decision
Always maximise monetary benefit
questions.explanation: Satisficing reflects bounded rationality: actors settle for satisfactory solutions given cognitive and information limits.

questions.q: A 'veto player' in policy analysis is an actor whose agreement is:
options: Irrelevant to policy change
Required for a change in the status quo
Only needed at evaluation
Limited to the judiciary
questions.explanation: Veto players are individual or collective actors whose consent is necessary to alter the policy status quo; more of them impede change.

questions.q: In appraisal, sensitivity analysis is conducted to:
options: Guarantee the project succeeds
Remove all uncertainty
Set the political agenda
Test how results change when key assumptions (e.g., discount rate) vary
questions.explanation: Sensitivity analysis checks the robustness of conclusions by varying uncertain parameters and observing the effect on results.

questions.q: The choice of discount rate in cost-benefit analysis is important because a higher rate:
options: Increases the weight given to future benefits
Reduces the present value of benefits that occur far in the future
Has no effect on long-term projects
Only affects costs, not benefits
questions.explanation: Higher discount rates shrink the present value of distant benefits, disadvantaging long-horizon projects such as climate action.

questions.q: Command-and-control regulation is characterised by:
options: Financial incentives that let firms choose how to comply
Legally binding standards with penalties for non-compliance
Voluntary information disclosure only
Government direct ownership of production
questions.explanation: Command-and-control uses mandatory rules and standards backed by sanctions, contrasting with market-based incentive instruments.

questions.q: A Pigouvian tax is a policy instrument designed to:
options: Subsidise polluting industries
Correct a negative externality by pricing the social cost
Fund only administrative overhead
Replace all regulation
questions.explanation: A Pigouvian tax internalises externalities, such as pollution, by making producers pay for the social harm they cause.

questions.q: 'Nudges', in the behavioural approach to policy instruments, work by:
options: Mandating behaviour with heavy penalties
Banning undesirable options entirely
Providing large cash subsidies
Altering choice architecture to steer decisions while preserving freedom of choice
questions.explanation: Nudges use defaults, framing and other choice-architecture changes to influence behaviour without removing options or strong incentives.

questions.q: An 'epistemic community' influences policy primarily through:
options: Control of the national budget
Shared expert knowledge and authoritative claims about a problem area
Ownership of media outlets
Military authority
questions.explanation: Epistemic communities are networks of experts whose recognised knowledge shapes how problems and solutions are understood.

questions.q: Formative evaluation is best described as evaluation that:
options: Occurs only after a programme ends to judge overall success
Takes place during development or early delivery to improve the programme
Measures only monetary returns
Sets the legislative agenda
questions.explanation: Formative evaluation feeds back during design or early implementation to refine and strengthen the intervention.

questions.q: A logic model or theory of change in policy design typically links:
options: Only inputs to costs
Inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes and impact in a causal chain
Stakeholders to their incomes
Discount rates to tax rates
questions.explanation: A theory of change/logic model articulates the causal pathway from resources and activities through to intended outcomes and impact.

questions.q: When cost-benefit analysis yields a benefit-cost ratio greater than 1, it indicates that:
options: Costs exceed benefits
Discounted benefits exceed discounted costs
The project must be rejected
The discount rate is negative
questions.explanation: A benefit-cost ratio above 1 means present-value benefits outweigh present-value costs, supporting the case for the project.

questions.q: A key reason cost-effectiveness analysis is widely used in health policy is that it:
options: Requires no data on costs
Ignores which intervention is cheaper
Only compares financial returns
Avoids assigning a monetary value to health outcomes
questions.explanation: CEA lets analysts compare interventions by cost per health outcome (e.g., per DALY averted) without monetising life or health directly.

questions.q: In behavioural economics, the concept of 'bounded rationality' introduced by Herbert Simon refers to the idea that decision-makers:
options: Have cognitive limits and often 'satisfice' rather than optimise
Ignore prices when making choices
Always maximise utility given perfect information
Behave irrationally in all economic decisions
questions.explanation: Bounded rationality holds that limited cognition, information, and time lead people to seek satisfactory ('satisficing') rather than optimal outcomes.

questions.q: The tendency to rely too heavily on the first piece of information encountered when making decisions is called:
options: Mental accounting
Framing
Hyperbolic discounting
Anchoring
questions.explanation: Anchoring occurs when an initial reference value disproportionately influences subsequent judgments and estimates.

questions.q: A farmer estimates flood risk as high mainly because a severe flood happened last year and is easy to recall. This illustrates the:
options: Endowment effect
Representativeness heuristic
Availability heuristic
Sunk cost fallacy
questions.explanation: The availability heuristic makes people judge probability by how easily instances come to mind, overweighting recent or vivid events.

questions.q: According to prospect theory, developed by Kahneman and Tversky, people evaluate outcomes relative to:
options: The average income of their community
Absolute final wealth levels
Expected utility maximisation only
A reference point, with losses looming larger than gains
questions.explanation: Prospect theory holds that value is assessed as gains and losses from a reference point, and losses are weighted more heavily than equivalent gains.

questions.q: Loss aversion means that, roughly, the pain of losing a given amount is:
options: Equal to the pleasure of gaining the same amount
Smaller than the pleasure of an equivalent gain
About twice as strong as the pleasure of an equivalent gain
Irrelevant to decision-making
questions.explanation: Empirical estimates suggest losses feel roughly twice as painful as equivalent gains are pleasurable, a hallmark of loss aversion.

questions.q: A 'nudge', as defined by Thaler and Sunstein, is an intervention that:
options: Alters choices without forbidding options or significantly changing incentives
Mandates a specific behaviour through law
Removes all but one option from a choice set
Imposes financial penalties for undesired behaviour
questions.explanation: A nudge steers behaviour predictably while preserving freedom of choice and without materially changing economic incentives.

questions.q: The set of ways in which choices can be presented and organised to influence decisions is called:
options: Marginal analysis
General equilibrium
Revealed preference
Choice architecture
questions.explanation: Choice architecture is the design of the environment in which people make decisions, including defaults, ordering, and framing.

questions.q: Automatically enrolling workers into a pension scheme (while allowing opt-out) dramatically raises participation mainly because of the power of:
options: Default options and status quo bias
Higher financial returns
Tax penalties for non-enrollment
Mandatory contribution laws
questions.explanation: People tend to stick with pre-set defaults due to inertia and status quo bias, so default enrollment sharply increases participation.

questions.q: Present bias (also called hyperbolic discounting) describes the tendency to:
options: Overweight immediate rewards relative to future ones, causing time-inconsistency
Discount all periods at a constant exponential rate
Ignore the timing of rewards entirely
Value future rewards more than immediate ones
questions.explanation: Present bias means people place disproportionate weight on the present, leading to procrastination and time-inconsistent plans like undersaving.

questions.q: Mental accounting refers to the tendency of people to:
options: Always compute the opportunity cost of every rupee
Treat money as non-fungible by assigning it to separate mental categories
Keep formal double-entry books for household finances
Ignore how money is labelled or sourced
questions.explanation: Mental accounting means people mentally segregate money into accounts (e.g. 'grocery' vs 'savings'), violating the economic assumption that money is fungible.

questions.q: The framing effect occurs when:
options: Incentives are doubled
People are given complete information
Logically equivalent descriptions of a choice lead to different decisions
The order of options is randomised
questions.explanation: Framing effects arise because presenting the same facts differently (e.g. as a gain vs a loss) changes people's choices.

questions.q: A health message stating '90% of patients survive this surgery' versus '10% of patients die' is an example of:
options: Anchoring
Mental accounting
Positive versus negative framing
The endowment effect
questions.explanation: The two statements are logically identical but the survival (positive) frame typically makes the surgery seem more acceptable: a classic framing effect.

questions.q: The endowment effect is the tendency to:
options: Prefer endowments from the government
Spend windfall income faster than earned income
Value things more highly simply because one owns them
Undervalue inherited assets
questions.explanation: The endowment effect means ownership raises the perceived value of a good, so people demand more to give it up than they would pay to acquire it.

questions.q: System 1 and System 2, as popularised by Kahneman, refer respectively to:
options: Fast, automatic, intuitive thinking and slow, effortful, deliberate thinking
Short-run and long-run supply
Government and market decision systems
Micro and macroeconomics
questions.explanation: System 1 is fast and intuitive; System 2 is slow and analytical, and many biases arise from over-reliance on System 1.

questions.q: The representativeness heuristic can lead people to:
options: Ignore base rates by judging probability from resemblance to a stereotype
Rely only on statistical data
Overweight sample size
Always compute correct conditional probabilities
questions.explanation: Judging likelihood by how much something resembles a prototype causes base-rate neglect and conjunction errors.

questions.q: The 'sunk cost fallacy' describes the tendency to:
options: Overinvest in new projects only
Discount future costs excessively
Continue an endeavour because of already-invested resources that cannot be recovered
Ignore all past costs when deciding
questions.explanation: The sunk cost fallacy leads people to 'throw good money after bad' by honouring irrecoverable past investments rather than assessing marginal costs and benefits.

questions.q: In the Save More Tomorrow (SMarT) programme, employees commit in advance to allocate part of future pay raises to savings. This design primarily exploits:
options: Anchoring on the interest rate
The availability heuristic
Loss aversion by cutting current take-home pay
Present bias, inertia and loss aversion by deferring the pain and using defaults
questions.explanation: SMarT overcomes present bias by scheduling saving in the future, avoids felt losses by tying it to raises, and uses automatic escalation (default inertia).

questions.q: Reminders sent via SMS to encourage savings deposits are effective largely because they counter:
options: Limited attention and forgetting (inattention)
Risk aversion
Loss aversion
The endowment effect
questions.explanation: Reminders address limited attention, a cognitive constraint whereby people simply forget to act on their intentions.

questions.q: The concept of 'libertarian paternalism' advocated by Thaler and Sunstein means:
options: Leaving markets entirely unregulated
Steering people toward welfare-improving choices while preserving freedom to choose
Banning harmful products outright
Mandating behaviours deemed good for citizens
questions.explanation: Libertarian paternalism tries to influence choices for people's own good while still allowing them to opt out: the philosophical basis of nudging.

questions.q: A common ethical criticism of nudging is that it:
options: Always costs more than regulation
Never changes behaviour
Is illegal in most countries
Can be manipulative and bypass people's conscious, deliberate reasoning
questions.explanation: Critics argue nudges may covertly exploit biases, undermining autonomy and transparency by influencing people without their reflective consent.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a 'sludge' rather than a nudge?
options: A default green-energy tariff
Placing healthy food at eye level
A reminder to take medication
Excessively complex paperwork that deters people from claiming benefits they are entitled to
questions.explanation: Sludge is friction in choice architecture that obstructs behaviour in people's interest, such as burdensome forms that reduce benefit take-up.

questions.q: Deworming and immunisation uptake in field experiments rose sharply when small in-kind incentives (like lentils) were offered. This suggests that health behaviour can be blocked by:
options: High monetary prices only
Complete lack of demand
Small hassle costs and present bias, which modest incentives help overcome
Cultural prohibitions alone
questions.explanation: Banerjee et al.'s work in India showed tiny incentives offset present bias and small frictions, sharply raising immunisation rates.

questions.q: The 'planning fallacy' is the tendency to:
options: Overestimate the time and cost a task will require
Underestimate the time, costs and risks of future actions while overestimating benefits
Plan too far into the future
Avoid making any plans
questions.explanation: The planning fallacy leads people and institutions to systematically underestimate completion times and costs, a common cause of project overruns.

questions.q: 'Choice overload' refers to the finding that offering too many options can:
options: Eliminate all decision biases
Guarantee optimal decisions
Always increase satisfaction and purchases
Reduce the likelihood of any choice being made and lower satisfaction
questions.explanation: Excessive options can paralyse decision-makers and reduce satisfaction, so simplifying choice sets is a common choice-architecture tactic.

questions.q: In prospect theory, the value function is:
options: Linear over all outcomes
Flat everywhere
Convex for gains and concave for losses
Concave for gains and convex for losses, and steeper for losses
questions.explanation: The S-shaped value function shows diminishing sensitivity (concave gains, convex losses) and a steeper slope for losses, capturing loss aversion.

questions.q: Weather-indexed crop insurance often has low uptake among farmers partly because premiums are paid now for an uncertain future payout, a pattern explained by:
options: The endowment effect only
Perfect rationality
Present bias and the salience of upfront costs versus abstract future benefits
Excessive numeracy
questions.explanation: Farmers overweight the immediate, certain premium relative to a delayed, uncertain benefit, reflecting present bias and low trust/salience issues.

questions.q: The 'default effect' is powerful in organ donation rates because opt-out (presumed consent) countries have far higher donation registration than opt-in countries. This is chiefly due to:
options: Mandatory donation laws
Inertia and the implicit endorsement conveyed by the default
