Higher incomes in opt-out countries
Stronger altruism in opt-out countries
questions.explanation: Defaults harness inertia and are read as a recommended choice, so switching the default dramatically changes participation without coercion.

questions.q: Social norm messaging (e.g. 'most households in your area pay taxes on time') is effective because people are influenced by:
options: Only financial penalties
Descriptive social norms: what others actually do
Anchoring on tax rates
Mental accounting
questions.explanation: Descriptive norms leverage the tendency to conform to observed majority behaviour, a technique used in tax-compliance nudges.

questions.q: Overconfidence bias in policy contexts most commonly manifests as:
options: Overestimating the accuracy of one's judgments and forecasts
Underestimating one's own knowledge and abilities
Excessive risk aversion
Perfect calibration of probabilities
questions.explanation: Overconfidence leads decision-makers to place too much certainty in their estimates, contributing to forecasting and project-planning errors.

questions.q: The finding that people spend windfall or 'bonus' income more freely than regular earned income is best explained by:
options: Fungibility of money
Mental accounting, where money is labelled by its source
Loss aversion
The availability heuristic
questions.explanation: Mental accounting causes people to treat differently labelled money non-interchangeably, spending 'windfall' accounts more loosely.

questions.q: A 'cooling-off period' required before finalising certain purchases or loans is a choice-architecture tool designed to counter:
options: Impulsive, present-biased decisions made in a 'hot' state
The endowment effect
Loss aversion
Excessive deliberation
questions.explanation: Mandatory delays give System 2 time to override impulsive System 1 choices driven by present bias or emotional arousal.

questions.q: In behavioural terms, 'salience' as a policy lever means:
options: Reducing the number of choices
Increasing monetary incentives
Hiding prices from consumers
Making relevant information or costs more noticeable to guide attention
questions.explanation: Salience interventions draw attention to information (e.g. energy labels, tax-inclusive prices) so it influences decisions.

questions.q: The 'IKEA effect' describes the tendency to:
options: Place higher value on things one has partially created or assembled
Avoid self-assembly products
Prefer flat-packed goods
Undervalue one's own labour
questions.explanation: The IKEA effect is a labour-based extension of the endowment effect: people overvalue outcomes they helped build.

questions.q: Which best describes 'confirmation bias'?
options: Updating beliefs fully with new evidence
Confirming decisions with a supervisor
Seeking and interpreting information in ways that confirm pre-existing beliefs
Preferring confirmed reservations
questions.explanation: Confirmation bias is the tendency to favour evidence that supports one's existing views and to discount contradictory evidence.

questions.q: Commitment devices, such as locked savings accounts (e.g. SEED in the Philippines), help people by:
options: Eliminating present bias entirely through education
Removing all savings options
Increasing interest rates
Voluntarily restricting future choices to overcome self-control problems
questions.explanation: Commitment devices let present-biased individuals bind their future selves, and studies found locked accounts raised savings balances.

questions.q: A key limitation of nudges compared to regulation or taxation is that nudges:
options: Always cost more than mandates
Often produce small effect sizes and may not address structural or large-scale problems
Are ineffective for every behaviour
Cannot be evaluated experimentally
questions.explanation: Nudge effects, while cheap, are often modest and may be insufficient for problems requiring strong incentives or systemic reform.

questions.q: The 'peanuts effect' in mental accounting refers to:
options: Preferring peanuts as a snack
Avoiding small purchases
Treating small amounts of money as trivial and spending them carelessly
Saving small amounts diligently
questions.explanation: The peanuts effect describes discounting the significance of small sums, leading to careless cumulative spending.

questions.q: In the context of agricultural fertiliser use, offering farmers free delivery and the option to buy at harvest time (when cash is available) rather than at planting time addresses:
options: Overconfidence
Present bias and liquidity/timing constraints
Loss aversion only
The representativeness heuristic
questions.explanation: Duflo, Kremer and Robinson's Kenya work showed small, well-timed nudges around cash availability and convenience raised fertiliser adoption.

questions.q: The 'status quo bias' is the tendency to:
options: Prefer that things remain the same and stick with current arrangements
Always pick the newest option
Choose randomly among options
Constantly seek change
questions.explanation: Status quo bias is a preference for the current state, which underpins the strong influence of defaults.

questions.q: Which of the following is the clearest example of a 'framing' nudge in health policy?
options: Banning tobacco sales
Labelling food with traffic-light colours (red/amber/green) for nutritional content
Subsidising gym memberships
Taxing sugary drinks
questions.explanation: Traffic-light labels reframe nutritional information into an intuitive, salient format that guides choices without restricting them.

questions.q: 'Hyperbolic discounting' differs from standard 'exponential discounting' because it produces:
options: No discounting of the future
Preference reversals as the timing of rewards approaches
A constant discount rate over time
Time-consistent preferences
questions.explanation: Hyperbolic discounting implies steeply falling discount rates over short horizons, causing preferences to reverse and generating self-control problems.

questions.q: The behavioural insight that people are more motivated to avoid losing a bonus already 'granted' than to earn the same bonus is used in teacher-incentive experiments through:
options: Increasing base salaries
Reducing class sizes
Randomising pay
Framing incentives as losses (clawback) rather than gains
questions.explanation: Fryer et al. found that giving teachers money upfront and clawing it back for underperformance (loss framing) outperformed traditional bonuses.

questions.q: 'Anchoring' can be used constructively in fundraising by:
options: Hiding suggested amounts
Removing all donation options
Presenting a higher suggested donation to raise the reference point for giving
Offering only one fixed amount
questions.explanation: Suggested-amount anchors shift donors' reference points, and higher (plausible) anchors tend to increase average contributions.

questions.q: A behaviourally informed critique of purely 'rational actor' models in development policy is that they:
options: Overstate the role of emotions
Cannot be tested empirically
Assume unlimited cognition, willpower and self-interest that real people lack
Ignore prices and incentives completely
questions.explanation: The World Development Report 2015 argued that people 'think automatically, think socially, and think with mental models,' departing from the rational-actor benchmark.

questions.q: In the 2015 World Development Report 'Mind, Society, and Behavior', the three principles of human decision-making are thinking automatically, thinking socially, and:
options: Thinking with mental models shaped by society and culture
Thinking rationally
Thinking individually
Thinking financially
questions.explanation: The WDR 2015 framework identifies automatic thinking, social thinking, and thinking through culturally derived mental models.

questions.q: Making a desired action the 'active choice' (requiring people to explicitly choose yes or no) is a middle path between opt-in and opt-out that:
options: Guarantees higher enrollment than opt-out
Is identical to mandating the behaviour
Removes freedom of choice
Forces a deliberate decision without setting a default
questions.explanation: Required active choice compels an explicit decision, avoiding default manipulation while still prompting engagement with the option.

questions.q: Behavioural research on poverty (Mullainathan and Shafir) suggests that scarcity of money or time:
options: Has no effect on cognition
Imposes a cognitive 'bandwidth tax' that can worsen decisions
Only affects the wealthy
Improves decision-making by focusing the mind fully
questions.explanation: Their 'scarcity' research shows that preoccupation with pressing needs consumes mental bandwidth, reducing cognitive capacity for other decisions.

questions.q: A well-designed impact evaluation of a nudge should ideally use:
options: Only administrative cost data
A randomised controlled trial (RCT) comparing treatment and control groups
Anecdotal testimonials
The policymaker's intuition
questions.explanation: RCTs provide credible causal estimates of a nudge's effect by randomly assigning exposure, the gold standard in behavioural policy testing.

questions.q: The main reason 'financial literacy training' alone often fails to change savings behaviour, according to behavioural evidence, is that:
options: Savings behaviour is fully rational
Knowledge does not automatically overcome present bias, inertia and self-control problems
Training is always too expensive
People already know everything about finance
questions.explanation: Information gaps are only part of the problem; behavioural barriers like present bias and inertia require structural nudges, not just knowledge.

questions.q: Which statement best captures a balanced view of nudges for development practitioners in South Asia?
options: Nudges can complement but rarely replace incentives, regulation and structural reforms
Nudges never work in low-income settings
Nudges are a complete substitute for public investment
Nudges eliminate the need for evaluation
questions.explanation: Behavioural interventions are low-cost complements that work best alongside, not instead of, incentives, regulation and structural policy.

questions.q: In Acemoglu and Robinson's framework, what primarily distinguishes 'inclusive' from 'extractive' economic institutions?
options: Inclusive institutions secure broad property rights and open economic opportunity to the many, while extractive institutions channel resources to a narrow elite
Inclusive institutions have lower tax rates than extractive institutions
Inclusive institutions require democracy while extractive institutions require dictatorship
Inclusive institutions rely on foreign aid while extractive ones rely on natural resources
questions.explanation: Inclusive institutions enforce property rights and provide a level playing field for broad participation, whereas extractive institutions concentrate income and power in the hands of an elite.

questions.q: Rent-seeking is best defined as:
options: Collecting rent from tenants on agricultural land
Investing in new technology to raise productivity
Saving income for future consumption
Expending resources to capture existing wealth or secure privileges rather than creating new value
questions.explanation: Rent-seeking uses real resources to obtain economic rents through privilege or redistribution rather than producing new wealth, making it socially wasteful.

questions.q: According to Mancur Olson's 'The Logic of Collective Action', why do large groups often fail to organise for their shared interest?
options: Large groups are always legally prohibited from organising
Members lack the intelligence to understand their interest
Individuals have an incentive to free-ride on the efforts of others since benefits are non-excludable
Governments subsidise small groups but not large ones
questions.explanation: When a collective benefit is non-excludable, each member gains whether or not they contribute, so rational individuals free-ride and the group under-provides collective action.

questions.q: A principal-agent problem in governance arises because:
options: Principals always have more information than agents
Citizens and officials always share identical goals
There is no way to design incentives for public officials
Agents (officials) may pursue their own interests, and principals (citizens) cannot fully observe or control their actions
questions.explanation: The problem stems from misaligned incentives combined with information asymmetry: the agent knows more about their effort than the principal can monitor.

questions.q: 'Elite capture' of a development programme refers to:
options: The recruitment of elites into government service
A training programme aimed at future leaders
The disproportionate control of programme benefits or decisions by locally powerful individuals
The taxation of wealthy households to fund the poor
questions.explanation: Elite capture occurs when locally dominant actors divert the benefits or decision-making of a programme toward themselves at the expense of intended beneficiaries.

questions.q: Which statement best captures a key risk of decentralisation in weak-institution settings?
options: It can worsen elite capture if local accountability mechanisms are weak
It always eliminates corruption by moving power closer to people
It guarantees more equal distribution of public goods
It removes the need for any central government
questions.explanation: Decentralisation brings decisions closer to citizens but can entrench local elites where local checks, transparency, and electoral competition are weak.

questions.q: Secure property rights are argued to promote growth mainly because they:
options: Guarantee that the state owns all productive assets
Eliminate the need for contracts and courts
Automatically redistribute wealth to the poor
Encourage long-term investment by assuring people they can keep the returns
questions.explanation: When people are confident their returns will not be expropriated, they invest, innovate, and accumulate capital over longer horizons.

questions.q: 'State capacity' most directly refers to a state's ability to:
options: Effectively implement policies, raise revenue, and enforce laws across its territory
Hold elections on schedule
Maintain a large standing army
Attract foreign investment through low wages
questions.explanation: State capacity is the administrative, fiscal, and coercive ability to carry out policy (collect taxes, deliver services, and enforce rules) throughout the country.

questions.q: Olson's concept of the 'encompassing interest' suggests that:
options: An actor controlling a large share of the economy internalises more of the social costs of its predation
Encompassing groups never engage in rent-seeking
Only foreign investors have encompassing interests
Small narrow-interest groups always benefit society
questions.explanation: An encompassing organisation or ruler that captures much of the economy has an incentive to limit its own predation because it bears a large share of the resulting losses.

questions.q: Which best describes 'accountability' in the World Development Report 2004 service-delivery framework?
options: The total budget allocated to a sector
Relationships in which one actor can demand answers and impose consequences on another for performance
The number of civil servants employed by a ministry
The frequency of cabinet reshuffles
questions.explanation: Accountability links actors through delegation, financing, performance, information, and enforceability: allowing consequences to be applied for poor service delivery.

questions.q: In the WDR 2004 model, the 'short route' of accountability runs from:
options: Providers to central auditors
Politicians to international donors
Clients (users) directly to service providers
Citizens directly to politicians through elections
questions.explanation: The short route is direct client power over providers (e.g., user feedback and choice), contrasted with the long route through politicians and policymakers.

questions.q: 'Political settlement' analysis emphasises that institutions function according to:
options: The formal wording of laws alone
The number of NGOs operating in a country
The underlying distribution of power among elites and groups in society
International credit ratings
questions.explanation: Political settlement analysis holds that whether formal institutions are enforced depends on how they align with the real balance of power among contending groups.

questions.q: North, Wallis and Weingast describe a 'limited access order' as one in which:
options: Everyone has equal access to organisations and markets
Trade is limited to a single port
Economic and political privileges are restricted to elites to manage violence
Access to the internet is legally restricted
questions.explanation: In limited access orders, elites limit access to valuable rights and organisations, using the resulting rents to reduce incentives for violence among themselves.

questions.q: The 'resource curse' in political economy refers to the tendency for:
options: Natural-resource wealth to weaken institutions and fuel rent-seeking and conflict
Mineral exports to lower a country's exchange rate permanently
Resource-rich countries to always grow fastest
Renewable resources to run out quickly
questions.explanation: Resource windfalls can undermine accountability, encourage rent-seeking and corruption, and finance conflict, often leaving resource-rich states worse governed.

questions.q: Why can corruption persist even when most people consider it harmful?
options: Because it can be a self-reinforcing equilibrium where individuals expect others to be corrupt
Because it has no effect on individual incentives
Because auditors always approve of it
Because it is legally protected in most countries
questions.explanation: Corruption is often a coordination trap: when everyone expects bribery to be the norm, deviating is costly, sustaining a bad equilibrium.

questions.q: A 'developmental state' is typically characterised by:
options: An absence of any industrial policy
Complete public ownership of all firms
A competent, relatively autonomous bureaucracy that guides industrialisation with embedded ties to business
A weak bureaucracy that avoids intervening in markets
questions.explanation: Developmental states combine bureaucratic capacity and autonomy with 'embedded' links to the private sector to steer structural transformation, as in East Asia.

questions.q: Peter Evans's concept of 'embedded autonomy' means a bureaucracy is:
options: Randomly staffed through patronage
Fully controlled by private firms
Isolated from society and unaccountable
Connected to social actors yet insulated enough to pursue coherent goals
questions.explanation: Embedded autonomy pairs dense networks with business (embeddedness) and corporate coherence/insulation (autonomy), enabling effective industrial policy.

questions.q: Which is a classic collective-action solution proposed by Elinor Ostrom for managing common-pool resources?
options: Community-designed rules with monitoring, graduated sanctions, and conflict-resolution mechanisms
Abandoning the resource entirely
Full privatisation is the only viable option
Complete central-government control in every case
questions.explanation: Ostrom showed local users can sustainably self-govern commons through clearly defined boundaries, locally crafted rules, monitoring, graduated sanctions, and dispute resolution.

questions.q: 'Clientelism' as a mode of politics is best described as:
options: A merit-based civil service examination
Exchange of targeted material benefits for political support, often conditioned on loyalty
Provision of public goods to all citizens equally
Independent judicial review of contracts
questions.explanation: Clientelism trades particularistic benefits (jobs, transfers, favours) for votes or support, typically enforced through monitoring of recipients' loyalty.

questions.q: The main political-economy obstacle to reforms that create net gains is often that:
options: Reforms never produce winners
All citizens oppose any change
Reforms are always technically infeasible
Losers are concentrated and organised while winners are diffuse and hard to mobilise
questions.explanation: Concentrated losers who anticipate their losses can block reforms, while dispersed potential winners face collective-action problems in supporting them.

questions.q: Fernandez and Rodrik's 'status quo bias' shows that reforms can fail to be adopted even when a majority would gain, because:
options: Voters are irrational
Politicians never want reform
The reform is always inefficient
Individual uncertainty about who will win creates ex-ante opposition despite ex-post majority gains
questions.explanation: When individuals cannot know in advance whether they will personally gain, uncertainty can produce a majority against a reform that would ultimately benefit most.

questions.q: Which best defines 'grand corruption' as distinct from 'petty corruption'?
options: Grand corruption involves small bribes to frontline staff
Grand corruption is always legal
Grand corruption involves high-level officials distorting major policies or contracts for private gain
Petty corruption only occurs in rich countries
questions.explanation: Grand corruption operates at the top of government, capturing policy and large contracts, whereas petty corruption involves small everyday bribes at the point of service.

questions.q: A key insight of the 'good enough governance' critique is that:
options: All governance reforms must be pursued simultaneously
Reform priorities should be sequenced and context-specific rather than a long uniform checklist
Governance quality does not matter for development
Only rich countries need governance reform
questions.explanation: Merilee Grindle argued the exhaustive 'good governance' agenda is unrealistic; countries should prioritise a feasible, context-appropriate subset of reforms.

questions.q: 'Isomorphic mimicry' in state-building refers to states that:
options: Perfectly replicate the capacity of advanced states
Abolish formal institutions entirely
Reject all foreign institutional models
Copy the outward forms of effective institutions without gaining their function
questions.explanation: Pritchett, Woolcock and Andrews describe how states adopt the appearance of best-practice institutions to gain legitimacy while lacking real functionality.

questions.q: The 'capability trap' described by Andrews, Pritchett and Woolcock occurs when:
options: States rapidly build strong capability
Donors withdraw all funding
Citizens gain too much capability
Persistent adoption of reforms as signals leaves states stuck with low real implementation capacity
questions.explanation: The capability trap is a low-level equilibrium where reforms are adopted for legitimacy but real state capability stagnates or declines.

questions.q: Problem-Driven Iterative Adaptation (PDIA) recommends that reform:
options: Ignore local officials
Follow a fixed blueprint imported from abroad
Start from locally nominated problems and adapt through iterative learning
Be designed entirely by external consultants
questions.explanation: PDIA builds reform around locally defined problems, authorising experimentation and iterative feedback rather than transplanting external best-practice designs.

questions.q: In the political economy of tax, why is a broad tax base sometimes linked to better governance?
options: Because tax revenue cannot fund public goods
Because taxing citizens directly can strengthen the fiscal contract and demands for accountability
Because broad taxes eliminate the need for a bureaucracy
Because taxes always reduce state capacity
questions.explanation: When states rely on broad taxation of citizens rather than resource rents or aid, taxpayers have greater incentive and leverage to demand accountability: the 'fiscal contract'.

questions.q: 'Regulatory capture' occurs when:
options: A regulator is abolished by parliament
An agency meant to serve the public interest instead advances the interests of the firms it regulates
Consumers write the regulations
Regulation is enforced too strictly
questions.explanation: Regulatory capture arises when concentrated industry interests come to dominate a regulator's decisions, subordinating the broader public interest.

questions.q: Which mechanism best explains how information campaigns (e.g., publicising officials' performance) can reduce corruption?
options: By reducing information asymmetry so citizens can better sanction poor performers
By increasing officials' salaries automatically
By centralising all decisions
By removing elections entirely
questions.explanation: Transparency lowers the information asymmetry at the heart of the principal-agent problem, strengthening citizens' ability to detect and punish misconduct.

questions.q: The Ugandan public-expenditure tracking survey famously found that:
options: All education funds reached schools
A large share of non-wage funds intended for schools was captured before arrival, and publicity later reduced leakage
Corruption is impossible to measure
Schools received more than their allocation
questions.explanation: The PETS revealed major leakage of school grants; subsequent newspaper publication of entitlements sharply cut the diversion, illustrating information's power.

questions.q: An 'extractive' political institution, per Acemoglu and Robinson, tends to:
options: Concentrate power without constraints, enabling elites to set extractive economic rules
Guarantee independent courts
Always coexist with inclusive economic institutions
Distribute political power broadly and constrain rulers
questions.explanation: Extractive political institutions concentrate unconstrained power, which elites use to structure economic institutions that extract from the rest of society.

questions.q: Why might a ruling elite block productivity-enhancing innovation ('the fear of creative destruction')?
options: Because citizens dislike higher incomes
Because innovation never raises output
Because innovation is always illegal
Because new technologies can erode the elite's economic rents and political power
questions.explanation: Acemoglu and Robinson argue elites may resist innovation when it threatens the sources of their rents and their hold on power, even if it would grow the economy.

questions.q: 'Common-pool resources' differ from pure public goods because they are:
options: Rival (subtractable) but hard to exclude users from
Always privately owned
Non-rival and non-excludable
Never subject to overuse
questions.explanation: Common-pool resources are subtractable, one person's use reduces what's available, yet exclusion is difficult, creating the classic overuse dilemma.

questions.q: In Bardhan and Mookherjee's analysis, decentralisation improves targeting of anti-poverty spending mainly when:
options: Central bureaucrats have perfect information
Local governments are captured by elites
Local political competition and information advantages are strong relative to capture risks
There is no local information about the poor
questions.explanation: They model a trade-off: local governments know the poor better but may be captured; net benefits depend on the strength of local accountability versus capture.

questions.q: 'Yardstick competition' in decentralised governance refers to voters:
options: Ignoring performance altogether
Voting only on national issues
Measuring officials against a fixed physical standard
Comparing their local government's performance with neighbouring jurisdictions to judge incumbents
questions.explanation: Yardstick competition lets citizens use neighbouring jurisdictions as a benchmark, disciplining local incumbents by comparison.

questions.q: The 'Samaritan's dilemma' in the political economy of aid or relief describes:
options: Recipients always over-preparing
Anticipated assistance weakening recipients' own incentives to prepare or reform
A conflict between two donors
Donors never wanting to help
questions.explanation: If aid is expected regardless of behaviour, it can undercut incentives for self-protective or reform effort: a moral-hazard-style problem for benevolent givers.

questions.q: Which describes a 'de jure' versus 'de facto' distinction in political power?
options: De jure is real power; de facto is written power
De facto power only exists in democracies
De jure power comes from formal institutions/law; de facto power comes from resources, organisation, and force
They are identical concepts
questions.explanation: De jure power is allocated by formal rules, while de facto power derives from wealth, arms, and the ability to solve collective-action problems outside formal channels.

questions.q: 'Bureaucratic quality' as measured in governance indicators typically captures:
options: The frequency of elections
Meritocratic recruitment, insulation from political pressure, and predictable administration
The number of ministries
The size of the national debt
questions.explanation: Bureaucratic quality reflects merit-based hiring, professional autonomy, and rule-bound, predictable administration: correlates of effective policy implementation.

questions.q: The concept of 'veto players' (Tsebelis) helps explain why:
options: More independent actors whose agreement is needed for change makes policy change harder
Policy change is unrelated to institutional structure
Veto players only exist in autocracies
Fewer actors always block reform
questions.explanation: The more numerous and ideologically distant the actors whose consent is required, the smaller the set of feasible changes: raising status-quo stability.

questions.q: Why is measuring corruption with perception indices (e.g., CPI) methodologically limited?
options: Perceptions perfectly reflect actual bribery levels
Perceptions can lag reality, reflect bias, and conflate different corruption types
Indices are legally prohibited
Corruption is never perceived by anyone
questions.explanation: Perception-based measures may be shaped by reputation, media, and observer bias, and cannot cleanly separate petty from grand corruption or reflect recent changes.

questions.q: A 'political business cycle' refers to:
options: A cycle of trade fairs
Incumbents manipulating fiscal or monetary policy around elections to boost short-term popularity
The natural rhythm of stock markets
The rotation of business leaders in politics
questions.explanation: Political business cycles occur when officeholders time expansionary policy to elections to improve their re-election prospects, often at longer-term cost.

questions.q: In social-accountability practice, a 'community scorecard' primarily works by:
options: Replacing elected local governments
Setting national tax rates
Auditing central bank reserves
Enabling citizens and providers to jointly assess and negotiate service quality
questions.explanation: Community scorecards convene users and providers to rate services and agree improvements, strengthening the short route of accountability.

questions.q: The 'free-rider problem' is most acute for goods that are:
options: Excludable and rival
Purely private
Non-excludable, so contributors cannot prevent non-contributors from benefiting
Always provided by markets efficiently
questions.explanation: When benefits cannot be withheld from non-payers, individuals have little incentive to contribute, leading to under-provision of the good.

questions.q: Which best captures the 'natural state' concept in North, Wallis and Weingast?
options: A state existing only in nature reserves
A state without any government
The default social order historically, using rent creation among elites to limit violence
A fully open-access democracy
questions.explanation: The 'natural state' (limited access order) is the historically dominant form that manages violence by distributing rent-generating privileges among powerful elites.

questions.q: Why can anti-corruption drives that only raise penalties sometimes fail?
options: Because without changing monitoring and the underlying incentive equilibrium, expected punishment stays low
Because higher penalties always eliminate corruption instantly
Because corruption is unrelated to incentives
Because penalties never deter anyone
questions.explanation: Deterrence depends on the probability of detection times the penalty; if monitoring and enforcement are weak, higher nominal penalties leave expected costs low.

questions.q: 'Second-generation' fiscal federalism stresses that decentralisation outcomes depend heavily on:
options: Ignoring local officials' incentives
Eliminating intergovernmental transfers
Only the number of local governments
The incentives created by how revenues, spending, and borrowing responsibilities are assigned
questions.explanation: Second-generation theory focuses on political and fiscal incentives facing sub-national officials, hard budget constraints and revenue-expenditure alignment, rather than benevolent planners.

questions.q: A 'soft budget constraint' for sub-national governments creates a risk that they will:
options: Never receive any transfers
Overspend or over-borrow, expecting central bailouts
Fully internalise fiscal costs
Always balance their budgets
questions.explanation: If localities anticipate rescue by the centre, they face weak incentives for fiscal discipline, encouraging excessive spending and debt.

questions.q: The idea that 'institutions are the fundamental cause of long-run growth' (as argued in institutionalist literature) contrasts most directly with explanations centred on:
options: Contract enforcement
Geography and culture as the deep determinants
Property rights
Political power
questions.explanation: Institutionalist accounts position institutions as the deep driver, contrasting with rival hypotheses that emphasise geography or culture as primary.

questions.q: 'Coproduction' of public services refers to:
options: Producing goods only for export
Citizens actively contributing to producing services alongside state providers
Privatising all services
Two governments merging
questions.explanation: Coproduction, associated with Ostrom, involves users and officials jointly generating outcomes, such as community policing or participatory sanitation, improving effectiveness.

questions.q: Which is the most accurate statement about the relationship between electoral democracy and corruption?
options: Elections can discipline officials but may fail to curb corruption where information, party competition, or judicial independence are weak
Democracies are always more corrupt than autocracies
Elections automatically eliminate corruption
Voting has no effect on official behaviour
questions.explanation: Elections provide an accountability mechanism, but their effectiveness against corruption depends on informed voters, competitive parties, a free press, and independent courts.

questions.q: In labour economics, the 'informal sector' is best characterized by which feature?
options: Only agricultural wage labour
Work outside the ambit of formal regulation, social protection, and often without written contracts
Employment covered by written contracts and social security
Jobs paying above the statutory minimum wage
questions.explanation: Informality refers to work that falls outside formal regulatory frameworks, lacking social protection and often written contracts.

questions.q: Roughly what share of India's total workforce is estimated to be in informal or unorganized employment?
options: About 60 percent
About 20 percent
About 40 percent
About 90 percent
questions.explanation: Estimates consistently place around 90 percent of India's workforce in informal employment, one of the highest shares globally.

questions.q: 'Frictional unemployment' refers to joblessness arising from which cause?
options: A general deficiency of aggregate demand in the economy
A mismatch between workers' skills and available job requirements
Seasonal fluctuations in agricultural activity
The normal time it takes workers to search for and match with jobs
questions.explanation: Frictional unemployment is the short-term joblessness that occurs as workers search for and transition between jobs.

questions.q: 'Structural unemployment' is most directly caused by which of the following?
options: Workers voluntarily leaving jobs to find better ones
A recession reducing overall demand for goods
The time lag in processing job applications
A mismatch between workers' skills or location and available jobs, often due to technological or sectoral change
questions.explanation: Structural unemployment stems from a mismatch between the skills/location of workers and the requirements of available jobs.

questions.q: 'Disguised unemployment' in agriculture describes a situation where:
options: More workers are employed than needed, so their marginal product is near zero
Workers hide their employment status to claim benefits
Workers are actively searching but cannot find any work
Seasonal workers are idle between harvests
questions.explanation: Disguised unemployment occurs when the marginal productivity of some workers is effectively zero because more people work than the task requires.

questions.q: The classic 'monopsony' argument suggests that a minimum wage can, under certain conditions:
options: Have no effect on either wages or employment
Increase both wages and employment when a single employer dominates the labour market
Always reduce employment regardless of market structure
Only benefit employers at the expense of workers
questions.explanation: Under monopsony, where an employer has wage-setting power, a well-set minimum wage can raise wages without reducing (and may increase) employment.

questions.q: In a competitive labour market, standard theory predicts that a minimum wage set above the equilibrium wage will:
options: Leave employment unchanged
Reduce the labour supply to zero
Create a surplus of labour (unemployment) as quantity supplied exceeds demanded
Increase employment
questions.explanation: Above equilibrium, a price floor causes quantity supplied to exceed quantity demanded, producing unemployment in the standard competitive model.

questions.q: The Card and Krueger (1994) New Jersey fast-food study is famous for challenging which conventional belief?
options: That tariffs raise domestic prices
That minimum wage increases necessarily reduce employment
That trade always benefits both partners
That inflation and unemployment are unrelated
questions.explanation: Card and Krueger found little to no employment decline after a minimum wage hike, challenging the textbook competitive prediction.

questions.q: David Ricardo's principle of comparative advantage holds that a country should specialize in goods for which it has:
options: The largest population of workers
The lowest opportunity cost of production
The highest export tariffs
The lowest absolute production cost
questions.explanation: Comparative advantage rests on relative opportunity cost, not absolute cost: countries gain by specializing where their opportunity cost is lowest.

questions.q: Under the theory of comparative advantage, mutually beneficial trade is possible even when one country:
options: Has an absolute advantage in producing every good
Has no natural resources
Imposes no tariffs
Uses a fixed exchange rate
questions.explanation: Even if one country is absolutely more productive in all goods, differences in relative (comparative) advantage still make trade beneficial for both.

questions.q: An import tariff on a good typically has which combination of effects in the importing country?
options: Lower domestic price, higher imports
No change in price but higher imports
Lower domestic price, government revenue loss
Higher domestic price, lower imports, and government revenue
questions.explanation: A tariff raises the domestic price, reduces the quantity imported, and generates revenue for the government.

questions.q: Compared to a tariff, an import quota that restricts quantity generally does NOT directly generate:
options: Protection for domestic producers
Government tax revenue (unless licenses are auctioned)
Reduced import volumes
A higher domestic price
questions.explanation: Unlike a tariff, a quota's scarcity rents usually accrue to license holders rather than as government revenue, unless licenses are auctioned.

questions.q: 'Import Substitution Industrialization' (ISI) is a development strategy that emphasizes:
options: Producing goods domestically to replace imports, often behind protective barriers
Focusing solely on primary commodity exports
Maximizing exports of manufactured goods
Eliminating all industrial policy
questions.explanation: ISI seeks to build domestic industry by substituting locally produced goods for imports, typically protected by tariffs and controls.

questions.q: 'Export-Oriented Industrialization' (EOI), associated with the East Asian 'tigers', is characterized by:
options: Heavy reliance on protecting the domestic market from imports
Prohibiting foreign investment
Focusing exclusively on agriculture
Orienting production toward competitive export markets to drive industrial growth
questions.explanation: EOI centers on producing for and competing in world export markets, credited with rapid growth in economies like South Korea and Taiwan.

questions.q: The 'infant industry' argument for protection contends that:
options: Protection should target only agriculture
All industries should be permanently protected
Mature industries deserve subsidies over new ones
New industries need temporary protection until they mature and become competitive
questions.explanation: The infant industry argument holds that emerging domestic industries may need temporary protection to reach efficient scale and competitiveness.

questions.q: In India, the four consolidated Labour Codes (2019-2020) merged 29 central labour laws into codes covering wages, industrial relations, social security, and:
options: Monetary policy
Foreign trade
Occupational safety, health and working conditions
Agricultural pricing
questions.explanation: The fourth code is the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, alongside the Wages, Industrial Relations, and Social Security codes.

questions.q: The 'Code on Wages, 2019' notably introduced the concept of:
options: Wages paid only in kind
Abolition of all minimum wages
A statutory national floor wage applicable across India
Fixed wages tied to export earnings
questions.explanation: The Code on Wages provides for a national floor wage below which state minimum wages should not fall, and universalizes minimum wage coverage.

questions.q: A key criticism of India's earlier Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (Chapter V-B) was that firms with 100+ workers needed government permission to:
options: Retrench, lay off, or close units
Export their products
Pay bonuses
Hire new workers
questions.explanation: The provision required prior government approval for layoffs, retrenchment, or closure in larger firms, often blamed for discouraging formal hiring.

questions.q: 'MSME' in the Indian policy context stands for:
options: Ministry of State and Municipal Enterprises
Managed Sector Marketing Establishments
Market System for Manufacturing Exports
Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises
questions.explanation: MSME refers to Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises, a sector central to employment and output in India.

questions.q: India's 2020 revised MSME classification bases enterprise categories on:
options: Investment in plant/machinery and annual turnover
Export volume only
Number of employees only
Age of the enterprise
questions.explanation: The 2020 revision introduced a composite criterion combining investment in plant and machinery/equipment with annual turnover.

questions.q: The primary rationale for a 'minimum wage' from a policy standpoint is to:
options: Maximize government revenue
Increase the profits of large firms
Encourage informality
Set a wage floor to protect workers from exploitation and ensure a basic living standard
questions.explanation: Minimum wages aim to establish a floor that protects low-paid workers from exploitation and supports a minimum standard of living.

questions.q: A 'living wage' differs from a 'minimum wage' primarily in that a living wage:
options: Applies only to public sector workers
Is set by employers voluntarily
Aims to cover the cost of a decent standard of living, not just legal subsistence
Is always lower than the minimum wage
questions.explanation: A living wage is intended to meet basic needs for a decent standard of living, often exceeding the statutory minimum wage.

questions.q: The 'Lewis model' of development describes economic growth driven by:
options: Elimination of the informal sector by decree
Transfer of surplus labour from a traditional (agricultural) sector to a modern (industrial) sector
Reduction of the industrial workforce
Rising agricultural tariffs
questions.explanation: Arthur Lewis's dual-sector model explains growth through the movement of surplus labour from subsistence agriculture into the modern industrial sector.

questions.q: The 'labour force participation rate' (LFPR) measures the share of:
options: The working-age population that is either working or actively seeking work
The total population that is employed
Firms that hire formal workers
Employed workers who are unionized
questions.explanation: LFPR is the proportion of the working-age population that is either employed or actively looking for work.

questions.q: India's female labour force participation rate has been notably low and, until recent upticks, was often reported around:
options: Exactly 50 percent
Around 20-25 percent
Above 60 percent
Over 70 percent
questions.explanation: India's female LFPR has historically been low, frequently reported in the low-to-mid 20s percent range, though recent PLFS data show increases.

questions.q: 'Cyclical unemployment' rises and falls with:
options: The seasons of the agricultural year
The number of new graduates each year
The business cycle and aggregate demand
The level of the minimum wage only
questions.explanation: Cyclical unemployment moves with the business cycle, increasing during recessions when aggregate demand falls.

questions.q: A 'labour union' (trade union) primarily functions to:
options: Collectively bargain for workers' wages, benefits, and working conditions
Determine import tariffs
License new businesses
Set national monetary policy
questions.explanation: Trade unions organize workers to bargain collectively over pay, benefits, and conditions, strengthening workers' negotiating position.

questions.q: 'Collective bargaining' refers to:
options: Negotiation between organized workers (via a union) and employers over terms of employment
Individual workers negotiating salaries one-on-one
Consumers negotiating product prices
Government setting all wages centrally
questions.explanation: Collective bargaining is the process by which unions and employers negotiate wages, hours, and working conditions on behalf of workers.

questions.q: The 'terms of trade' for a country refers to:
options: Its tariff rate on imports
The number of trade agreements it has signed
The ratio of export prices to import prices
The total volume of its exports
questions.explanation: Terms of trade is the ratio of a country's export prices to its import prices; improvement means more imports can be bought per unit of exports.

questions.q: The 'Prebisch-Singer hypothesis' argues that over the long run:
options: Free trade always equalizes incomes
Tariffs improve global welfare
The terms of trade of primary commodity exporters tend to deteriorate relative to manufactures
Manufactured goods prices fall relative to primary commodities
questions.explanation: Prebisch and Singer argued that prices of primary commodities tend to decline relative to manufactured goods, hurting commodity-dependent exporters.

questions.q: A 'deadweight loss' from a tariff represents:
options: The revenue collected by the government
The gain to domestic producers
The net loss to society from reduced trade efficiency not captured by anyone
The subsidy paid to exporters
questions.explanation: Deadweight loss is the reduction in total surplus, efficiency lost to distorted production and consumption, that no party captures.

questions.q: The 'Stolper-Samuelson theorem' predicts that trade liberalization tends to benefit:
options: The abundant factor of production, while hurting the scarce factor
The scarce factor of production in a country
All workers equally
Only the government
questions.explanation: Stolper-Samuelson holds that trade raises the return to a country's abundant factor and lowers the return to its scarce factor.

questions.q: For a labour-abundant developing country, the Heckscher-Ohlin framework predicts it will tend to export:
options: Labour-intensive goods
Capital-intensive goods
Only raw commodities regardless of factor endowments
Financial services exclusively
questions.explanation: Heckscher-Ohlin predicts countries export goods that intensively use their abundant factor: labour-abundant nations export labour-intensive goods.

questions.q: 'Skilling India' / the Skill India Mission primarily aims to address which labour market problem?
options: The skills gap and low employability of the workforce
Excessive union membership
Excess capital
Overvaluation of the currency
questions.explanation: Skill India seeks to raise employability by training workers to close the gap between industry needs and workforce skills.

questions.q: The 'demographic dividend' refers to the potential economic boost from:
options: A rise in the retirement age
A large working-age population relative to dependents, if productively employed
A declining birth rate reducing the labour force
An aging population needing more pensions
questions.explanation: The demographic dividend is the growth potential when the working-age share of the population is large: realized only if those workers are productively employed.

questions.q: MGNREGA (India's rural employment guarantee) primarily provides:
options: Unemployment insurance to all citizens
A legal guarantee of up to 100 days of wage employment per rural household per year
Export subsidies to farmers
Guaranteed factory jobs in cities
questions.explanation: MGNREGA legally guarantees up to 100 days of unskilled manual wage work per year to each rural household that demands it. The Act was repealed from 1 July 2026 and replaced by the Viksit Bharat G RAM G Act 2025, which raises the guarantee to 125 days.

questions.q: A 'wage subsidy' to employers is intended to:
options: Reduce the number of formal jobs
Increase import tariffs
Raise the cost of hiring workers
Lower the effective cost of employing workers and encourage hiring
questions.explanation: A wage subsidy reduces the employer's cost of labour, incentivizing more hiring, especially of targeted groups.

questions.q: The concept of 'jobless growth' describes an economy where:
options: Both output and jobs fall together
Employment grows faster than output
Output/GDP grows but employment fails to expand proportionately
Only public sector jobs increase
questions.explanation: Jobless growth occurs when GDP rises without a commensurate increase in employment, a concern in several developing economies including India.

questions.q: 'Premature deindustrialization', discussed by Dani Rodrik, refers to:
options: Rapid growth of manufacturing employment
The rise of heavy industry in rich nations
Agriculture replacing services
Developing countries' manufacturing sectors peaking at lower income levels than earlier industrializers
questions.explanation: Rodrik's premature deindustrialization describes developing economies whose manufacturing share peaks earlier and at lower income levels than historical industrializers.

questions.q: A 'non-tariff barrier' (NTB) to trade could include:
options: A direct sales tax on domestic goods
Quotas, licensing requirements, or technical/sanitary standards used to restrict imports
An ad valorem import tax
A floating exchange rate
questions.explanation: NTBs are trade restrictions other than tariffs: quotas, licensing, standards, and similar measures that limit imports.

questions.q: The 'World Trade Organization' (WTO) principle of 'Most Favoured Nation' (MFN) requires members to:
options: Give the best trade terms only to their closest ally
Extend to all members any trade advantage granted to one member
Ban trade with non-members
Impose the highest tariff on all imports
questions.explanation: MFN requires that a trade concession granted to one WTO member be extended equally to all other members, ensuring non-discrimination.

questions.q: 'Backward linkages' from an industry refer to its demand for:
options: Final consumer goods
Foreign currency reserves
Inputs and supplies from upstream domestic suppliers
Export markets abroad
questions.explanation: Backward linkages arise when an industry creates demand for inputs from upstream domestic suppliers, spurring their growth.

questions.q: The 'Production Linked Incentive' (PLI) scheme in India is a form of industrial policy that offers:
options: Tariffs on all imports
Guaranteed government jobs
Financial incentives tied to incremental domestic production/sales in targeted sectors
Subsidized consumer loans
questions.explanation: PLI schemes provide incentives linked to incremental production or sales to boost manufacturing in strategic sectors.

questions.q: 'Contract labour' arrangements are often criticized in labour policy because they can:
options: Allow firms to avoid direct employment obligations and reduce worker security
Raise wages above the minimum
Guarantee permanent employment
Strengthen union bargaining automatically
questions.explanation: Contract labour lets principal employers avoid direct obligations, often leaving workers with lower job security and weaker protections.

questions.q: The 'efficiency wage' theory suggests employers may pay above-market wages to:
options: Comply with tariff rules
Reduce their total wage bill
Boost worker productivity, reduce turnover, and discourage shirking
Increase unemployment
questions.explanation: Efficiency wage theory holds that paying above-market wages raises productivity and morale while lowering turnover and shirking.

questions.q: A key argument AGAINST permanent import protection is that it can:
options: Force domestic firms to become more efficient
Always lower consumer prices
Increase export competitiveness automatically
Create inefficient, uncompetitive industries dependent on protection ('rent-seeking')
questions.explanation: Prolonged protection can shelter inefficiency, encourage rent-seeking, and leave industries unable to compete internationally.

questions.q: The 'gains from trade' in economics arise primarily from:
options: One country exploiting another
Specialization according to comparative advantage and exchange, expanding total output
Governments collecting tariff revenue
Reducing the number of goods produced globally
questions.explanation: Gains from trade come from countries specializing where they have comparative advantage and exchanging, raising total output and consumption.

questions.q: 'Social security' provisions for informal workers are difficult to implement mainly because:
options: Formal firms refuse all contributions
Informal workers lack formal employer records, regular contracts, and identifiable contributions
There is no demand for such protection
Informal workers earn too much
questions.explanation: The absence of formal employment records, regular contracts, and traceable contributions makes extending social security to informal workers challenging.

questions.q: The 'reservation wage' is the:
options: Wage set aside for future payment
Wage reserved for government employees
Maximum wage an employer will pay
Lowest wage at which a worker is willing to accept a job
questions.explanation: The reservation wage is the minimum wage at which an individual is willing to accept employment rather than remain unemployed.

questions.q: A common critique of 'export processing zones' (EPZs / SEZs) is that they may:
options: Offer tax breaks and relaxed labour rules that can weaken worker protections
Raise tariffs on domestic goods
Always create high-quality permanent jobs with strong labour rights
Prohibit any foreign investment
questions.explanation: EPZs/SEZs often grant tax concessions and relaxed regulations to attract investment, sometimes at the cost of weaker labour protections.
